entries.title: Housing Action Illinois sues HUD as Trump administration brands nonprofit 'radical left NGO'
entries.summary: <p>A federal judge temporarily blocked the Trump administration's efforts to cut roughly $56 million in housing counseling funding — giving Chicago-based Housing Action Illinois and nine other nonprofits across the U.S. some relief.</p><p>The victory comes after the 10 nonprofits sued the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development on Tuesday for attempting to claw back funding allocated for HUD's Comprehensive Housing Counseling program. The program was created by Congress to provide consumers with first-time homebuyer education classes, foreclosure prevention assistance and other services.</p><p>The Democracy Defenders Fund and Jacobson Lawyers Group filed the lawsuit on behalf of the organizations, which includes the National Urban League, North Carolina Housing Coalition, New Jersey Citizen Action, Housing & Community Development Network of NJ, National CAPACD, Fair Housing Resource Center, Southwest Fresno Community Development Corporation, Somerville Community Corporation and the National Foundation for Debt Management.</p><p>The attorneys filed a temporary restraining order Wednesday, urging the court to extend the deadline for the funds’ allocation. The funds would have expired Wednesday had the court not intervened.</p><p>U.S. District Judge Jia Cobb ruled late Wednesday that suspending the deadline was necessary so the nonprofits and the government could have more time to argue their case.</p><p>“The Court is hesitant to determine whether the government is required to obligate nearly $60 million without the government itself being fully heard on the issue,” Cobb wrote in her decision. “However, the Court is likewise hesitant to allow September 30 to pass such as that Plaintiffs would lose out on significant amounts of funding due to allegedly unconstitutional actions.”</p><p>The nonprofits said in their <a class="Link" href="https://www.democracydefendersfund.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/092926_DDF-Complaint-National-Urban-League.pdf" target="_blank" >complaint</a> that the funds were illegally being withheld because they expressed views rejected by the Trump administration, violating First Amendment protections. And "to punish grantees," President Donald Trump used a pocket rescission to block congresionally appropriated funds. </p><p>In a news release last week announcing the rescission package, the White House claimed a number of nonprofits receiving HUD funds were peddling diversity, equity and inclusion practices and discriminating against people based on their race.</p><p>The release went on to call out Housing Action Illinois, saying the nonprofit was “a radical left NGO [nongovernmental organization] that believes ‘housing is a human right,’ and is committed to ‘advancing equitable community development and affirmatively furthering racial justice.’” The rescission included $1.5 million that was allocated to Housing Action Illinois.</p><p>The government opposed Cobb's suspension, arguing the court doesn’t have the power to override deadlines established by Congress. </p><p>Both parties will have a chance to present their case later this month, after the government submits a more detailed response to the nonprofits’ lawsuit.</p><p>Sharon Legenza, executive director of Housing Action Illinois, said the nonprofit was “very relieved” the temporary restraining order was granted. Keeping the funds in play means the nonprofits can continue to provide housing counseling support, and they may get reimbursed for services dating back to October 2025 — the start of the federal government’s fiscal year.</p><p>The 40-year-old nonprofit has done a “wide variety” of work to help people access safe and quality homes, Legenza said. </p><p>In fiscal year 2024, Housing Action Illinois’ housing counseling network served more than 12,500 households, according to a court declaration written by David Young, the nonprofit's director of capacity building. Almost 1,400 households that were served purchased their first home, and nearly 430 households evaded or resolved a mortgage default. In 2025, more than 750 participants from across the nation attended Housing Action Illinois’ housing counseling training, according to Young.</p><p>As part of its work, the group serves as an intermediary for HUD’s Comprehensive Housing Counseling program. It applies for the funding, then doles it out as subgrants among its 38 subgrantees.</p><p>Housing Action Illinois’ subgrantees work across eight states and Washington, D.C., to provide housing services to residents, according to Legenza.</p><p>“As we think about … inflation and just the increased cost of housing generally, more and more people are feeling stretched, and more and more people are looking to get assistance to help them figure out how are they going to be able to maintain their housing,” she said. “That's what housing counseling agencies do.”</p>

entries.title: Man, 63, charged with fatally shooting his sister in Auburn Gresham, police report says
entries.summary: <p>A man faces murder charges after an argument apparently led him to fatally shoot his older sister Wednesday afternoon in the Auburn Gresham neighborhood, according to a Chicago police report. </p><p>Randy Washington, 63, was arguing with Dorothy Washington, his 70-year-old sister, inside a residence in the 1900 block of West 83rd Street at 3:18 p.m., when he allegedly shot her in the chest, according to a police report obtained by the Sun-Times. </p><p>Washington, who was arrested at the scene, was charged with one felony count of first-degree murder and is scheduled to appear in court Friday.</p><p>A sibling of the two was on the scene and spoke to police, the report said. </p><p>Dorothy Washington was pronounced dead at 3:25 p.m., according to the Cook County medical examiner's office. <br></p>

entries.title: White Sox ready for ALDS showdown with Guardians that will be 'one to remember'
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> won their season series (seven games to six) against the division rival Guardians. But couldn’t hold them off in a late-September three-game set at Cleveland, or the American League Central standings as the Guardians won 24 of their last 34 games.</p><p>“It’s going to be one to remember,” reliever <b>Grant Taylor</b> said to the Sun-Times about this weekend’s ALDS matchup. “We’re going to go in and try to win two games at their place.”</p><p>It’s a playoff showdown that feels inevitable because the regular-season battle feels unresolved. Are the standings flipped if the fly ball Guardians infielder<b> Brayan Rocchio</b> lifted off Taylor found <b>Sam Antonacci</b>’s glove? Or was the level of baseball Cleveland reached down the stretch simply a cut above the rest of the division?</p><p>“We can beat Cleveland,” said general manager <b>Chris Getz</b>. “We’ve proven that we can. But they are definitely a team that’s been here before, and we respect them.”</p><p>The sides have disparate strengths.</p><p>The Sox followed up leading the AL in runs scored by chasing two Astros starters before they could complete the first inning, whereas the Guardians’ offense finished 11th, even with a late-season kick.</p><p>The Guardians flaunt a deep rotation and will throw likely AL Cy Young finalist <b>Parker Messick</b> in Game 1, followed by league strikeout leader <b>Gavin Williams</b> in Game 2. The Sox’ reliance on their bullpen will be strained over a best-of-five series and manager <b>Will Venable</b> laughed at the idea of having their Game 1 starter determined during Wednesday’s postgame celebration.</p><p>As much as the Sox celebrated guaranteeing a home playoff game by reaching this round, they will need to win at Progressive Field to advance, where they dropped four of seven in the regular season. It’s always the slimmest margin between these two.</p><p>But where the White Sox’ strong first half was reliant on dominance at home to offset struggles on the road, a postseason triumph in Houston has them feeling differently.</p><p>“All we need is our dugout,” said shortstop <b>Colson Montgomery</b>. “We love our fans and we love everyone that comes and travels and supports us. But it's about our dugout. We need each other and believe in each other.”</p><h3><b>Hicks on a heater</b></h3><p>Houston native <b>Jordan Hicks </b>was letter-perfect pitching in his hometown, retiring all 10 Astros he faced over his two Wild Card series appearances, striking out four.</p><p>After a rocky start to the year, Hicks raised his arm slot while sidelined with a lat strain, and found it restored the riding action on his four-seam fastball. His sinker also sinks less in turn, but forcing hitters to guess between two different types of triple-digit fastballs offset the loss.</p><p>Moreover, the newfound consistency of his delivery at this release point has made him a reliable option.</p><p>“I'm in a better position just throwing strikes at 100 to 102 mph versus trying to reach back for 103, 104 mph and then kind of spraying it a little bit, losing the feel,” Hicks said.</p><p>Being able to dial down to <i>just</i> 102 mph is a good place to be.</p><h3><b>ABS wizardry</b></h3><p>The White Sox preach being aggressive on challenges with the automated ball and strikes system (ABS), and are prouder of leading MLB in challenge rate than worried about being worst in success rate.</p><p>Catcher <b>Kyle Teel</b> balanced both in Houston, going 5-for-5 on challenges over two games.</p><p></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/01/white-sox-manager-will-venable-doesnt-fear-mistakes-and-his-team-is-fearless-in-return" >White Sox manager Will Venable doesn’t fear mistakes, and his team is fearless in return</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: White Sox manager Will Venable doesn't fear mistakes, and his team is fearless in return
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> manager Will Venable doesn’t always say the right thing.</p><p>“Speaking is not really my thing as far as literally getting words out and effectively communicating,” Venable told the Sun-Times. “I say ‘um’ all the time. Sometimes I say words and I'm like, ‘Damn, that didn't come out right.’”</p><p>The second-year skipper has a book of tongue twisters he’ll return to for practice. As he entered into coaching, he recalls reaching out to his friend, A’s broadcaster Jenny Cavnar for help on his public speaking, and credits her for giving him opportunities to practice in radio interviews.</p><p>Even stories from teammates about times he showed leadership during his playing days described Venable as more of an effective communicator, aided by the gravitas that his work ethic lent him, rather than an eager one. Working a job defined by communication across the endless different branches of an MLB organization required an evolution, but still reflects someone who doesn’t talk for the sake of talking.</p><p>“We're kids when we play this game, and he's a fully grown, mature adult doing this now,” said Sox field coordinator Chris Denorfia, who played with Venable on the Padres. “[His communication style] is the same, but it's more finely-tuned. He extends that into the coaching room. He wants all of our messages to be short, to the point, no fluff.”</p><p>A byproduct that’s more intentional with time is the lack of obfuscation. Venable doesn’t mince words in a postgame interview when one of his many non-traditional, metric-guided moves doesn’t pan out. He wants all his communication that way.</p><p>“The first layer is me talking about how I messed up, right, that takes some heat off of [the players],” Venable said. “The second part is everyone is going to make mistakes, right? I'm going to make mistakes, players are going to make mistakes, everyone is going to make mistakes. We need to have an environment where it's okay to make mistakes, we're not going to crumble because we make mistakes. We're going to make mistakes the right way. You're going to be accountable to it.”</p><p>For a White Sox roster asked constantly about their lack of experience, the idea that growing pains or protracted struggles are inevitable, rather than a source of shame, is brought up a lot. As the Sox’ arrive to October, they’ve felt the absence of an overbearing presence.</p><p>“Will's the man,” said shortstop Colson Montgomery. “Having a manager like that where you can kind of turn off the baseball player and turn on just being like, a man, like bros talking pretty much. So I think that's kind of what I've appreciated a lot about him. His communication is great.”</p><p>“He's a voice to be heard and he says what he needs to say when there's something that we need to address,” said starter Sean Burke. “But I think, honestly, one of his best traits is he let's us be a lot.”</p><p>In early September, Venable said few members of his team had experienced the abasement of individual priorities that postseason baseball requires, but he assumed they’d handle it well.</p><p>In a Wild Card Series sweep in Houston, his defacto No. 3 starter Anthony Kay agreed to a bullpen assignment to get the biggest outs of the clinching game, Grant Taylor affirmed he was good for a Game 1 ninth inning that took him to a career-high 54 pitches, and Burke went viral for a quote to the Sun-Times asserting his commitment to the team in such intense terms that he had to affirm he does have a real family, beyond just his White Sox teammates.</p><p>“It’s easier to put your body on the line when you’ve got guys like this around you,” Taylor said postgame Wednesday, after confirming he wasn’t actually available to pitch in Game 2.</p><p>In this environment, the bigger risk is Venable’s players offering him more than they can actually handle. He hopes he’s established it’s good to be honest.</p><p></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/01/white-sox-ready-for-alds-showdown-with-guardians-that-will-be-one-to-remember" >White Sox ready for ALDS showdown with Guardians that will be ‘one to remember’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: 'Broadview Six' judge wants to put prosecutors under oath, keeps contempt charges on the table
entries.summary: <p>When federal prosecutors in Chicago assured a judge last spring<b> </b>they’d had no contact with the White House or top Justice Department officials about their pursuit of six Operation Midway Blitz protesters, U.S. District Judge April Perry<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/07/broadview-ice-kat-abughazaleh-chicago-midway-blitz" target="_blank" ><u>took them at their word</u></a>.</p><p>Those days are clearly over.</p><p>Rather, in a remarkable turn-the-tables moment that underscores the damage done to the feds’ credibility here, Perry<b> </b>concluded Thursday<b> </b>that<b> </b>further<b> </b>“under oath”<b> </b>fact-finding<b> </b>is needed in the tainted case of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>“Broadview Six”</u></a> — leaving open the possibility that she’ll name a special prosecutor to investigate U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros<b> </b>and others.</p><p>She did so at the end of an hourlong hearing<b> </b>in which she asked an attorney for Boutros’ office, point-blank, whether any of the prosecutors who worked on the politically charged case would invoke their Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination.</p><p>He said he didn’t know.</p><p>Eventually, Perry told the lawyers, “my sole focus, at this point, is on lack of candor, concealment of material facts, or other misconduct that occurred before me.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Regardless, the judge added, it<b> </b>“has to be under oath, under penalties of perjury.”</p><p>Still, she assured them, “I’m not reaching any conclusions today about what occurred.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" >What to know about the ‘Broadview Six’ scandal rocking Chicago’s federal courthouse</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The judge also concluded that the six former defendants who once faced a felony have no legal stake in what happens next. The judge also<b> </b>indicated<b> </b>Mecklenburg<b> </b>had excused grand jurors who disagreed with the feds’ case, a claim Mecklenburg denies.</p><p>Mecklenburg retired<b> </b>from the Justice Department<b> </b>last week <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/09/25/broadview-six-boutros-mecklenburg" target="_blank" ><u>in order to defend herself</u></a>.</p><p>Perry said she found “most problematic”<b> </b>the fact that the apparent misconduct was redacted out of transcripts<b> </b>initially given to her by Boutros’ office. The redactions were made after<b> </b>Mecklenburg withdrew from the case.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/09/25/broadview-six-boutros-mecklenburg" >‘Broadview Six’ prosecutor slams Boutros in resignation letter, saying he pushed doomed felony charges</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The prosecutors who remained – and nearly took it to trial – were<b> </b>William<b> </b>Hogan, Matthew<b> </b>Skiba<b> </b>and<b> </b>Andres<b> </b>Almendarez. During Thursday’s hearing, Boutros’ office was represented by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Maxwell<b> </b>Lisy<b> </b>and<b> </b>Nathaniel<b> </b>Whalen.</p><p>It wasn’t long ago that Chicago’s U.S. attorney’s office was considered one of the top tier in the nation. Perry <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/17/broadview-six-judge-april-perry-trump-vance" target="_blank" ><u>once served in the office</u></a> and helped prosecute Jon<b> </b>Burge, the late Chicago police commander tied to torture claims who was ultimately convicted of perjury.</p><p>President Joe Biden nominated<b> </b>Perry<b> </b>in 2023 to serve as Chicago’s top federal prosecutor. But <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2024/03/10/april-perry-us-attorney-john-lausch-jd-vance-confirmation-senate" target="_blank" ><u>her confirmation was blocked</u></a> by<b> </b>then-Sen. JD Vance, who is now vice president.</p><p>Boutros was initially named U.S. attorney <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/03/28/former-prosecutor-andrew-boutros-named-chicagos-interim-u-s-attorney" target="_blank" ><u>on a temporary basis</u></a> by then-Attorney General Pam<b> </b>Bondi<b> </b>in April 2025. Chicago’s federal judges <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2025/07/25/chicagos-federal-judges-choose-andrew-boutros-as-top-prosecutor" target="_blank" ><u>then chose Boutros</u></a><b> </b>to continue in the role on a more permanent basis in July 2025.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But Boutros’ office has been in crisis ever since Perry discovered<b> </b>apparent wrongdoing by Boutros’ staff in one of the most prominent cases to result from Midway Blitz, the Trump administration’s aggressive deportation campaign.</p><p>One year ago this week, Boutros’ office began to level various Blitz-related charges against defendants, only to see them <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" target="_blank" ><u>mostly collapse without convictions</u></a>.</p><p>Now, multiple judges have wondered aloud whether they could trust his office in the wake of the “Broadview Six” revelations. And Perry’s refusal to shoot down the idea of a special prosecutor means the specter of a criminal prosecution still hangs over his head and others.</p><p>While the feds might eventually appeal any action taken by Perry, none of the moves she made Thursday seemed likely to trigger a challenge.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/30/broadview-six-ice-trump-doj-justice-chicago-midway-blitz" >Selective prosecution claims in ‘Broadview Six’ case the result of ‘fevered paranoia,’ feds say</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Perry’s inquiry threatens to reach into the upper echelon of the Justice Department, though. She seemed particularly frustrated during Thursday’s hearing when she tried to pin a government lawyer down on<b> </b>a question seemingly answered by the feds earlier this year.</p><p>Did Trump administration officials in Washington interfere in the case?</p><p>Federal prosecutors wrote<b> </b>in a March court filing<b> </b>that there were “no communications of any nature from, to, or with anyone outside”<b> </b>Boutros’ office “regarding any investigatory or charging decisions.”<b> </b>The only exception, they wrote, were local FBI investigators.</p><p>“To be crystal clear, this specifically includes anyone in the White House and all components and offices of Main Justice,” Hogan, Skiba and<b> </b>Almendarez<b> </b>wrote, referring to Justice Department headquarters.</p><div They know that their law licenses in this case are on the line if they do them inappropriately.”</p><p>But Thursday,<b> </b>Whalen acknowledged those communications might exist after all. He said they would have occurred after the decision was made to file charges. Perry tried to pin down when that decision was made, though, given that it took multiple tries for prosecutors to convince grand jurors to indict.</p><p>At one point, Perry’s eyes went wide during Thursday’s hearing as Whalen tried to square his argument with the March court filing.</p><p>The judge said she’d been told “there’s nothing. No way, no how. And now, your argument has changed pretty significantly, and is ‘well, if there was something, it would be privileged.’”</p><p>“I don’t believe I said ‘there’s no way, no how communications,’” Whalen replied.</p><p>“You didn’t,” Perry shot back, emphasizing that the original claim came from prosecutors who nearly took the case to trial.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/06/01/broadview-six-midway-blitz-abughazaleh-straw-rabbit-perry-trump-ice-crime" >‘Broadview 6’ defendants reflect on case doomed by feds’ apparent misconduct: ‘We didn’t commit a crime’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The judge spent much of the hearing exploring her various options. For example, she asked Whalen who would oversee a special prosecutor. He told her that person would report to the attorney general, because it’s up to the executive branch “to enforce the criminal laws.”</p><p>When Whalen brought up the Justice Department’s Office of Professional Responsibility, Perry noted that it “doesn’t investigate criminal offenses.”</p><p>“I think we’ve got to take OPR out of the equation when we’re talking about a special prosecutor,” she said.</p><p>The pair also went back-and-forth on the legal standard used by the Justice Department for opening a criminal investigation, with Perry correcting Whalen along the way.</p><p>Eventually, Perry simply asked him, “why should the judge’s standard be higher than the Department of Justice’s?”</p>

entries.title: Jeanne Gang and a North Lawndale community garden among the honorees at architecture's Designight 2026
entries.summary: <p>The Humboldt Park Health Wellness Center — with its iridescent green and blue cladding, designed to match the colors of the Caribbean Sea — is among the buildings that took top honors Thursday at the AIA Chicago's Designight 2026 awards ceremony.</p><p>Chicago firm Studio Gang, led by Aqua Tower architect Jeanne Gang, was also given the architecture organization's 2026 Firm Award, which recognizes a firm's body of work over the last 10 years.</p><p>The awards were among 52 projects that were recognized at the Chicago chapter of the American Institute of Architects' yearly gala, held at the Harris Theater for Music and Dance in Millennium Park.</p><p>Long-dubbed the "Oscars of Chicago architecture," Designight recognizes the best projects by local architects.</p><p>The Humboldt Park Health Wellness Center, 2933 W. Division St., snagged the Design Excellence Honor Award in the medium-sized firm subcategory.</p><p>Built for Humboldt Park Health, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2025/02/28/humboldt-park-wellness-center-puerto-rican-culture-architecture-lee-bey" target="_blank" >the $30 million center</a> by the firm JGMA was lauded for a design that reflects Humboldt Park's Puerto Rican heritage.</p><p>With Studio Gang, the awards jury praised the firm's "impact and legacy [that] extends well beyond individual projects, encompassing global influence on sustainable design, public engagement, and the evolution of architectural practice."</p><p>The celebrated firm is known for a portfolio of work that includes Lakeshore East skyscrapers Aqua Tower and the St. Regis, as well as smaller projects like the Nature Boardwalk at Lincoln Park Zoo and the Lavezzorio Community Center in Auburn Gresham.</p><div Johnson won the 2026 Lifetime Achievement Award. entries.title: With White Sox-Guardians series scheduled to start in daylight, Blackout Game might be tough
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox can have another Blackout Game, but it might have to start in daylight.</p><p>MLB released the entire schedule for the divisional round of the playoffs Thursday. Games 3 and 4 of the Sox' series against the Guardians at Rate Field are scheduled for 3 p.m. Wednesday and 4 next Thursday, respectively. That doesn't make for prime blackout conditions, at least not until sunset around 6:30. If Game 4 is the only game that day, it will start at 7, offering some hope.</p><p>Games 1 and 2 in Cleveland are set for noon Saturday and 4 p.m. Monday, respectively. If necessary, Game 5 is scheduled for 4 p.m. Oct. 10 in Cleveland. If it's the only Game 5 that day, it will start at 7. All games will air on TBS and truTV and streaming service HBO Max. Alex Faust, analyst Ron Darling and reporter Lauren Jbara will call it.</p><p>Sox-Guardians games are scheduled to be the first games each day they're played, a sure sign that the league and networks have more desirable games later. The Rays-Yankees series, for example, has Games 2-5 scheduled for prime time at 7 p.m.</p><p>The Sox' first Blackout Game was the tiebreaker against the Twins for the 2008 American League Central title. Jim Thome's solo home run in the seventh inning was the only run of the game. The Sox brought the blackout back for Game 3 of the 2021 AL Division Series against the Astros, igniting a raucous crowd that saw the Sox win 12-6. <br></p>

entries.title: NFL commissioner Roger Goodell visits Illinois again for more Bears stadium talks with Gov. JB Pritzker
entries.summary: <p>Illinois is still moving the chains in stadium talks to keep the Bears from jumping the state line to Indiana, officials said Thursday.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker met with NFL commissioner Roger Goodell, Bears minority owner Pat Ryan and the top legislative leaders who have been wrangling for several years over the property tax incentives the team is seeking to break ground in Arlington Heights.</p><p>It was Goodell’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/14/bears-stadium-hammond-arlington-heights-report-roger-goodell-met-illinois-lawmakers-nfl-commissioner" target="_blank" ><u>second meeting</u></a> in as many months with Illinois officials, while Ryan — who bankrolled his namesake stadium opening later this week at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/10/01/northwestern-ryan-field-penn-state-wildcats-nittany-lions-evanston-friday-college-football" target="_blank" ><u>Northwestern University</u></a> — takes a more active role in negotiations with the state over Bears president Kevin Warren, who hasn’t made inroads in Springfield.</p><p>The conversation, held in Chicago, also included Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch and the Capitol’s top stadium negotiators, South Side state Sen. Bill Cunningham and downtown state Rep. Kam Buckner.</p><p>Pritzker’s office noted they’ve “remained in conversation with the Bears about their plans in Illinois throughout the summer,” since the team announced in June that they were shifting focus to Hammond, Indiana.</p><p>Sources familiar with Thursday’s discussion suggested there was no major breakthrough, but some optimism that common ground could be found before lawmakers return to Springfield in mid-November for the fall veto session. Further meetings are expected this month.</p><p>"The Governor and General Assembly leadership were glad to participate in a productive meeting focused on keeping the Bears in Illinois and protecting taxpayers,” Pritzker’s office said in a press release announcing the meeting.</p><p>"The NFL appreciated the opportunity to meet with Gov. Pritzker and legislative leaders today,” NFL spokesman Brian McCarthy said in a statement. “Timely action is essential as the Bears work to find a long-term stadium solution for the club and their fans."</p><p>A Bears spokesman had no additional comment.</p><p>Hoosier lawmakers have rolled out <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/02/26/bears-stadium-hammond-indiana-hammong-senate-passes-bill-27-arlington-heights-george-mccaaskey-kevin-warren-nfl" target="_blank" ><u>the red carpet</u></a> for the Bears with legislation that would pump upwards of a billion taxpayer dollars into a new stadium.</p><p>Earlier this year, the Illinois House passed a bill that would allow the Bears to negotiate a discounted payment in lieu of taxes with local taxing bodies, earning critical support from Chicago Democrats because it would’ve shared proceeds with homeowners as property tax rebates — but those returns were deemed “<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/04/bears-stadium-property-tax-relief-pritzker-negligible" target="_blank" ><u>negligible</u></a>.”</p><p>The Illinois Senate passed a separate bill that would allow municipalities to create their own stadium authorities to negotiate with teams, but it crumbled in the waning hours of spring session <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/31/bears-stadium-bill-springfield-arlington-heights-hammond-indiana" target="_blank" ><u>without a vote in the other chamber</u></a>.</p><p>The Bears turned their noses at both measures, but haven’t spelled out what they want from the state beyond “property tax certainty.”</p><p>Ryan, a billionaire with a 10% stake in the team, has helped improve the tenor of discussions that had stagnated between Illinois officials and Halas Hall, according to sources familiar with the talks.</p><p>Goodell has toured the potential stadium sites in Arlington Heights and Hammond. Without stating a preference, he has publicly urged the Bears to come to a resolution “soon” — but Illinois sources are taking his visits as an indication that the league thinks the team is better off in its original state.</p><p>The Bears have committed to putting $2 billion into a new stadium wherever they end up. They’re under lease at Soldier Field until 2033.</p><p><i>Contributing: Sun-Times sports reporter Pat Finley</i></p>

entries.title: McHenry man sentenced to 12 years for battering infant son
entries.summary: <p>A McHenry man was sentenced to 12 years in prison for battering his then-infant son four years ago, according to the McHenry County state’s attorney’s office.</p><p>DeShawn M. Wilson, 28, pleaded guilty to a charge of aggravated battery to a child.</p><p>On July 17, 2022, paramedics responded to a call about an unresponsive infant, who was initially taken to Northwestern Medicine McHenry Hospital before being airlifted to Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children’s Hospital to treat a severe brain injury that required emergency surgery, prosecutors said.</p><p>Wilson had been caring for the 4-month-old child while his mother was at work, and admitted to police he had bounced and shaken the baby in an attempt to get him to sleep.</p><p>“This resolution holds Wilson accountable for the devastating and lasting injuries he caused his infant son,” McHenry County State’s Attorney Randi Freese said in a statement. “Our hope is that [the child’s family] can now move forward with their full attention where it belongs — on this child, his continued care, and his well-being.”</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: The dive after five overtimes: Lake View beats Von Steuben in rain-soaked thriller
entries.summary: <p>Early Thursday evening, everyone at Lane Stadium would have agreed that Lake View vs. Von Steuben was a crucial White North game.</p><p>When it finally ended at nearly 11 p.m., after five overtimes, the game had become much more.</p><p>“You are going to remember this night for the rest of your lives,” Lake View coach Kipp Duplechine told his team after their 36-34 victory.</p><p>Outside the stadium, a large Von Steuben player sobbed as his much smaller father hugged and consoled him, saying, “Sometimes that is how life is going to go.”</p><p>Both teams left everything on the field, battling each other and the constant rain. There were 13 fumbles. Lake View was 0-for-7 passing, and Von Steuben was 3-for-14.</p><p>Several large puddles lined the sideline, and some of the Wildcats dived into them to celebrate the win.</p><p>“It was hard,” Lake View running back Kaleb Lovett said. “I lost my voice I was yelling so much. I just thought of my coach’s voice telling me to keep going. I didn’t want to disappoint him.”</p><p>Lovett scored the game-winning two-point conversion after his five-yard, game-tying TD in the fifth overtime.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> That is what it takes, and that is what I was willing to do.”</p><p>Guallpa’s 18-yard touchdown run with 1:24 left in regulation tied the game at 22.</p><p>“It wasn’t the perfect conditions,” Guallpa said. “But as a team we stick together. The first half was rough, but we pulled it together at the end.”</p><p>Lovett had 25 carries for 296 yards and two touchdowns. His 56-yard TD early in the fourth quarter cut Von Steuben’s lead to 22-14.</p><p>"This is a beautiful game," Panthers coach Demetrius Hughes said. "There are highs and lows. My kids are fighters. They fight hard. I will rock with this team anytime."</p><p>Both teams fumbled the ball away in the first overtime. Lake View (6-1, 4-0) fumbled it away in the second overtime but then blocked Von Steuben’s field goal attempt to send the game to a third overtime. Both teams scored touchdowns with two-point conversions in the third overtime. Lovett was stopped at the goal line, and then Von Steuben missed a field goal to end the fourth overtime.</p><p>The Panthers scored on a six-yard pass from Christian Welk to Zidan Raya in the fifth overtime, but they came up short on the two-point conversion.</p><p>“For the first time I watched my kids fight and never stop,” Duplechine said. “I told them after the second overtime that even if we lose, I am proud of you guys. entries.title: Blackhawks already facing adversity after blowout loss to Mammoth
entries.summary: <p>SALT LAKE CITY — Any hopes that the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>' first-game struggles were largely due to quality of opponent were dashed Thursday.</p><p>In a 6-0 blowout loss against a solid but probably not elite Mammoth team, the Hawks looked even more discombobulated than they did <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/30/blackhawks-golden-knights-nhl-season-opener-patrick-kane" >Tuesday</a>.</p><p>It remains foolish to jump to conclusions after just two games (out of 84). The Sharks lost their first six games last season before becoming one of the NHL's most-improved teams, after all.</p><p>But if one did jump to conclusions now, they would likely be along these lines: the Hawks are the worst team of all time, they'll never make the playoffs again and perhaps the apocalypse is imminent.</p><p>That's how atrocious these two games have been.</p><p>"Obviously, [we] haven't seen our best hockey yet, by far," a tight-lipped Frank Nazar said. "So [we'll] continue to focus on the process and keep working towards that, because you know it's going to come."</p><p>Said a more loquacious Ian Cole: "I'm sure we're going to have a lot of conversations going forward here. We have a long flight ahead of us [to Buffalo]. I'm sure they'll be broached on that. It's not good enough. We think that we're a much better team than this."</p><p>The Hawks were consistently incapable of exiting their defensive zone Thursday, either because the Mammoth anticipated and intercepted their passes or because they missed their mark or whiffed on the puck entirely. </p><p>Coach Jeff Blashill said the Hawks made decisions "too slow," which was evident.</p><p>Two periods in, the Mammoth held an absurd 31-8 advantage in scoring chances (including 12-0 in high-danger chances). The Hawks' better third period was essentially irrelevant.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Mammoth goal: Anders Lee tips in a shot from the point. 4-0. <a href="https://t.co/drTt7D2azc">pic.twitter.com/drTt7D2azc</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2105855940670939528?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 2, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Bowen Byram, acquired to be the Hawks' new premier defenseman, was one of many players who especially struggled. </p><p>After Byram's pairing with Alex Vlasic was outshot 12-1 and conceded two goals in the first half of the game, Blashill moved him back to his natural left side, pairing him with Artyom Levshunov. The forward lines were also thoroughly shuffled, continuing this week's trend.</p><p>"I have tons of belief in these guys," Blashill said. "I said it when I took the job: 'You stay steady on the rudder.' Man, this is two games. ... Yes, we have urgency to go play a good hockey game on Saturday. But my focus is on us continuing to get better as a group. That doesn’t change."</p><h3><b>Bedard watch</b></h3><p>As other Blackhawks trickled off the ice following practice Wednesday, Connor Bedard was getting dressed to go on the ice by himself.</p><p>Bedard has been on the ice a lot lately, which seems like a good sign. But general manager Kyle Davidson isn't willing to commit yet to Bedard returning sooner than November, as originally estimated.</p><p>"We're just operating off the initial timeline," Davidson said Tuesday. "All along, we were going to find out new information, if anything, probably in October. Until we have that..."</p><h3><b>Energy management</b></h3><p>The Hawks held their usual pre-game meetings but didn't hold a morning skate Thursday.</p><p>It sounded like they might try minimizing morning skates this season, although the way things played out Thursday might change their minds.</p><p>"We just felt like, from an energy-management standpoint, we didn't want certain guys on the ice," Blashill said before the game. "And those guys were probably going on the ice if we gave them the option.</p><p>"It's one of the hard challenges of coaching in this league, trying to find that balance of when to practice, when to conserve energy. If you never practice, you lose your habits and probably your structure. If you practice all the time, you probably play tired. There's no easy solution to it."</p>

entries.title: Historic Avalon Regal Theater in play for $250,000 in repair funds
entries.summary: <p>The Avalon Regal Theater — the South Side's Moorish Revival jewel box that fell into decay after closing 16 years ago — is in line to get a $249,500 city grant to help fix up the landmark venue, the Chicago Department of Planning and Development announced Friday.</p><p>The cash from the agency's Adopt-A-Landmark Fund would help pay for critical masonry repairs and rebuild the exposed brick substructure of a tower on the northwest corner of the 99-year-old theater at 1645 E. 79th St.</p><p>Also covered under the grant would be the selective removal and resetting of displaced masonry, isolated repointing, temporary supplemental stabilization of the building and the isolated repairs on the theater's front facade, the department said.</p><p>The theater is among three projects recommended for a total of $666,400 in repair funding under the Adopt-A-Landmark program. entries.title: Charges pending after nearly 2-hour SWAT standoff in West Pullman
entries.summary: <p>An intoxicated man holed up inside a home who caused a nearly 2-hour long standoff is in police custody after firing a gun early Friday in West Pullman, police said. </p><p>Around 12:10 a.m. a SWAT incident was declared when a woman called 911 and officers responded to a home in the 12700 block of South Lowe Avenue where a drunken 47-year-old man she knows briefly left the home and fired multiple shots into the air before going back inside, Chicago police said. </p><p>The man willingly left the home around 1:45 a.m. and was arrested, police said. A gun was recovered at the scene and no one was hurt. </p><p>Charges have not been announced but are pending, police said. </p><p>Area 2 detectives are investigating. <br></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Man, 34, fatally shot in Portage Park smoke shop
entries.summary: <p>A gunman was seen running away from a Portage Park smoke shop after fatally shooting a man inside the business Thursday night. </p><p>Jefferson Park District officers on a traffic stop were flagged down by a witness who saw a suspicious person wearing a mask inside the smoke shop at 5612 W. Irving Park Rd. about 9:35 p.m., according to a Chicago police report obtained by the Sun-Times. </p><p>Inside they found a man, 34, who was unresponsive and suffering from a gunshot wound to the throat</p><p>The man, whose name was not released, was taken to Advocate Lutheran General Hospital in Park Ridge where he was pronounced dead at 10: 26 p.m., according to the Cook County medical examiner's office and police. </p><p>A witness saw a male gunman running moments after shots were fired, officials said. </p><p>No arrests have been made and police were searching for additional witnesses and video evidence. </p><p>Area 5 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Trump has been trashing election results, democracy from the start
entries.summary: <p>With the Supreme Court’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/09/14/supreme-court-rejects-trump-mail-ballot-restrictions-midterm-elections" >rejection</a> of Donald Trump's executive order curtailing mail-in voting, it seems certain he is ready to declare any Democratic victories in November as frauds. So it is particularly important to look back on that election Trump claimed was stolen from him.</p><p>No, I am not talking about his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2020/12/9/22166305/election-reform-death-threats-electoral-college-editorial" >7 million</a> vote loss to Joe Biden in 2020. It was long before that when Trump claimed Ted Cruz stole an earlier election: the Iowa Republican caucuses of 2016. </p><p>After Trump lost that election, he <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/realDonaldTrump/status/694879900256354304" target="_blank" >tweeted</a> “Ted Cruz didn’t win Iowa, he stole it. That is why all the polls were so wrong and why he got far more votes than anticipated. Bad!” Another <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/realDonaldTrump/status/694964856609439745" target="_blank" >tweet </a>that same day: “The State of Iowa should disqualify Ted Cruz from the most recent election on the basis that he cheated — a total fraud!” And <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/realDonaldTrump/status/694890328273346560" target="_blank" >another</a>: “Based on the fraud committed by Senator Ted Cruz during the Iowa caucus, either a new election should take place or Cruz results nullified.” In a radio interview that same day Trump <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2016/02/03/465459903/trumpertantrum-trump-says-cruz-cheated-in-iowa-wants-results-overturned" target="_blank" >announced</a> that he would “probably” sue over the results because what Cruz did was “unthinkable.” </p><p>What was the reaction? Remember, this was back in 2016 when Trump was simply a d-list celebrity who had been roasted on Comedy Central. As Cruz bluntly <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/story/2016/02/ted-cruz-donald-trump-denmark-218694" target="_blank" >stated</a>: “He’s losing it .... Who would be comfortable with someone who behaves this way having his finger on the button?.... We’re liable to wake up one morning and Donald, if he were president, would have nuked Denmark.” </p><p>So according to Trump, Democrats like Biden steal elections. And Republicans like Cruz steal elections. Frankly, anyone who ever defeats him has stolen the election. </p><p>So when Trump lost the 2020 election by 7 million votes, was anyone really surprised he denied it? The bigger the margin of defeat, the bigger the claims of fraud. </p><p>On Jan. 6, 2021 we learned what Trump would do in the event of an electoral loss. But a recurrence of this in January 2027 would be different in a very significant way: “peaceful protesters” would know in advance that they are backed by presidential pardons. </p><p>How does a democracy die? When candidates only accept election results they like. Period. Full stop. </p><p><i>Timothy P. O’Neill, professor emeritus, University of Illinois Chicago, School of Law</i></p><h3>Don’t let city off the hook</h3><p>Instead of celebrating the city of Chicago's weak clawback on the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/29/city-council-parking-meters-deal-compromise-stonepeak-partners" target="_blank" >parking meter deal</a>, maybe the Sun -Times should encourage deeper investigations on the no-bid contract of the law firm that originally handled the deal and it's subsequent<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2014/4/22/18546034/ex-mayor-daley-s-law-firm-losing-grip-on-city-hall-under-emanuel" target="_blank" >hiring</a> of former Mayor Richard M. Daley and other dubious activity.</p><p><i>Mike Sullivan, Avondale</i><br></p>

entries.title: Schmitt's Hawk 'gotcha' didn't fly the way he and fellow Republicans hoped
entries.summary: <p>Tuesday was supposed to be a big day for Missouri Sen. Eric Schmitt, a little-known first-term junior senator whose main claim to fame thus far was the 25 lawsuits he filed against President Joe Biden’s administration in a span of 20 months while Missouri’s attorney general.</p><p>But congressional hearings have long been a place not to do actual legislating but to make a name for oneself, and Schmitt was going to take his opportunity Tuesday, when he got to question former Special Counsel Jack Smith in the Senate Judiciary Committee.</p><p>Earlier that morning a short news item — just 80 words — popped up <a class="Link" href="https://www.axios.com/2026/09/29/eric-schmitt-jd-vance-vice-president-vp-2028" target="_blank" >on Axios</a>. The headline: “Sen. Eric Schmitt Is Drawing Buzz as a Possible Vance VP in 2028.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-530000" name="module-530000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>The body of the story, in part, read: “First-term Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) — who was a tough-on-crime state attorney general, and now is vice chair of the Joint Economic Committee — has grown close to Vice President Vance and is seen as a top prospect to become a potential 2028 running mate.</p><p>We hear the VP views Schmitt, 51, as trustworthy, intelligent, articulate and a deft political operator.”</p><p>I’ll let you draw your own conclusions about how that glowing — and unsourced — story ended up where it did on the morning of this hearing, but I think it’s safe to assume it wasn’t a coincidence.</p><p>Hours later, Schmitt was in the room where it happened, joining his fellow Republican lawmakers in punishing Smith for pursuing charges around Donald Trump’s 2020 election interference and his handling of classified documents.</p><p>And the theatrics were amped up to 11. Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., had already told Smith, “You make me want to throw up in my mouth.” </p><p>Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, proclaimed, “Javert from Les Mis would look at you with astonishment.” </p><p>Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., used her time to accuse Smith of bullying her late brother, Lindsey Graham.</p><p>Your taxpayer dollars at work, folks.</p><p>But anyway, this was all leading up to the big moment, when Schmitt was going to drop the smoking gun — alleged texts from someone in Smith’s office showing he was somewhere he shouldn’t have been and about to do something he shouldn’t have done.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/senator-eric-schmitt-jack-smith-basketball-perjury-rcna600546" target="_blank" >Except he wasn’t.</a> Smith wasn’t in Atlanta in February 2024 for an Atlanta Hawks game. He wasn’t in Atlanta at all. Instead, he’d been at a women’s college basketball game between the University of Maryland and the University of Iowa. Apparently, Schmitt confused the Hawks with the Hawkeyes.</p><p>It was an implosion of delicious proportions for the left, but at a time when Republicans and Trump are drowning in a midterm election hellscape of their own making, it also exposed just how desperate MAGA was for a win — any win.</p><p>Before Schmitt could finish imploding, MAGA media had already posted to socials their congratulatory dunks on Smith, unaware that the moment they’d been promised hadn’t gone the way it was supposed to.</p><p>Fox’s Sean Hannity deleted his post wherein “Schmitt puts Jack Smith on the spot,” and Benny Johnson deleted his (which misspelled the senator's name) saying “Schmidt just CAUGHT Jack Smith perjuring himself.”</p><p>The whole day, it seemed, from the Axios post in the morning, to the influencer posts in the afternoon, was designed to give the MAGA base some much-needed red meat amid a sea of bad poll numbers.</p><p>But it seems Republicans don’t have their priorities straight. They’ve given up on actual policy wins that could have helped stave off what may just be a blue monsoon in November, wins that were promised to voters two years ago. All they’ve got left are parlor tricks and subterfuge — and they can’t deliver on that, either.</p><p>It was a moment that was meant to go viral, and it did — but for all the wrong reasons.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2c0000" name="module-2c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Bears TE Cole Kmet begs Soldier Field fans to cooperate when team is on offense
entries.summary: <p>Late in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/28/bears-inactives-vs-eagles-k-cairo-santos-cb-tyrique-stevenson-good-to-go" >the Bears’ 27-7 win over the Eagles on Monday</a>, with the game well in hand, tight end <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/06/12/bears-te-cole-kmet-knows-the-secret-of-sticking-around-no-matter-who-comes-and-goes-at-halas-hall" >Cole Kmet</a> was waving frantically to the raucous crowd at Soldier Field to quiet down. He and his teammates could barely hear quarterback Case Keenum over the roar.</p><p>He’d love to see them make life that difficult for opposing offenses, but he pleaded — unprompted — for a little more cooperation when the Bears have the ball.</p><p>“P.S.A. to the fans: They need to be quiet when we’re on offense,” Kmet said. “It is ridiculous. It’s insane. I appreciate the energy, but take note from Minnesota how quiet it is when their guys are on offense.”</p><p>When Kmet and some other teammates tried signaling to the crowd to quiet down, it had no effect.</p><p>“I mean, I love the enthusiasm,” he said. “You can be as loud as you want on defense. It’s just that we’re trying to communicate and get off on the cadence and it’s hard to do that when the fans screaming on third-and-short. But it’s all good. I appreciate it.”</p><p>He's hoping they'll get on board Sunday when the Bears host the Jets.</p><p>Overall, it’s a good problem to have considering how lackluster the crowds were — with good reason — early in his career during the Matt Nagy and Matt Eberflus eras. The Bears no longer are getting booed off the field by their home crowd, but there appears to have been an overcorrection.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Trump's populist image goes poof
entries.summary: <p>As predictions of a blue wave swell, it's worthwhile to remember that polls are sometimes wrong, that surveys have tended to undercount Donald Trump voters (though they have been better in midterms), that professional prognosticators can err, and that Allan Lichtman is only right when he's lucky. And yet, if there has ever been a politician who has invited electoral repudiation by more thoroughly betraying his own voters than Trump has, I can't think of one.</p><p>Trump had the most zealous followers of anyone this side of Osama bin Laden, and in his first term, he did a certain amount of fan service. He cracked down on illegal (and legal) immigration, made gestures toward building a wall on the southern border, cut taxes, withdrew from the Iran nuclear deal and the Paris Climate Accords, and insulted and belittled everyone from Hillary Clinton to John Lewis.</p><p>Was there profiteering as well? Sure. Unlike his recent predecessors, Trump declined to place his assets in a blind trust. He assured the nation that his sons were keeping him out of the loop on all matters pertaining to the Trump Organization. His hotels became the go-to spots for favor-seekers both foreign and domestic. The Saudis practically camped out at one of them. But it was all pretty low-key compared with the sequel.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-350000" name="module-350000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>In his second term, Trump has been a caricature of a plutocrat, gilding the Oval Office, grinding the White House East Wing into dust to build his garish ballroom, plastering his name on everything in his line of sight, issuing commemorative coins with his face on them and vacuuming up wealth for himself and his family on a scale that has never been seen in American history. For his voters, by contrast, he has delivered higher prices, a shambolic mess of a war with Iran, tariffs that hit farmers particularly hard and an immigration crackdown that has caused Hispanic voters and even some podcast bros to recoil.</p><p>While some Trump opponents point to his cruelty and vulgarity as the selling points with his base, I demur. Clearly that's the case with some, but most people like to think they're on the side of the angels, not the devils. That's why whataboutism is the default answer to any objection. You cannot believe that you yourself are embracing the dark side, and so you must believe that the other side is worse.</p><p>Trump entered American politics as the <i>ur</i> populist. A huge part of his appeal was a familiar one in American politics — anti-corruption. It's a bitter irony now, but millions of Americans who supported Trump believed they were voting for cleaner government and bought his "drain the swamp" line. For decades, large numbers of Americans have believed that most politicians are crooked. In 2006, nearly 60% of Americans thought that "corruption is widespread throughout the government." In 2016, 59% of Americans rated the honesty/integrity of members of Congress as low or very low (but only half the country thought so little of senators).</p><p>Again and again in focus groups conducted by Sarah Longwell, voters offered that Trump was too rich to be bought. Michael from Arizona, who voted for Trump in 2016 but switched to Joe Biden in 2020, said in 2022, "I figured, OK, he can't be bought. He's got way too much money. So give him a chance." A two-time Trump voter from New Hampshire explained in 2024 that "He doesn't need to line his pockets with anything, so he doesn't have a hidden agenda. He's got his own money." Voters echoed this constantly. When you're convinced that the majority of politicians are in it for the money, who better than a billionaire to resist the special interests?</p><p>The myth was burnished by Trump's decision to forgo a government salary in his first term. Jim, a 2016 and 2020 Trump voter from Texas, said in February 2022: "I don't know that anybody else would stand up to (attacks and criticism) like that, and then give away their salary. ... The man worked for nothing for us, and took all of that beating all the time."</p><p>In August 2024, Carol, another two-time Trump voter from Michigan, mentioned with admiration: "He did not take a salary for it, and that kind of impressed me. Why ... is he doing this? He's not getting paid for it. Clearly has a passion for what he's doing."</p><p>It was the same with Greg from Georgia, who in June 2024 said, "He didn't need this. He was a billionaire. He was a successful businessman. He didn't need to do this."</p><h3>Anti-corruption myth unraveling </h3><p>Trump's second term has been a protracted demolition of his image as a populist every bit as thorough as the destruction of the East Wing. Though some voters recall his promise not to take a salary, it's tinged with irony now. Just this month, Janel, a 2024 Trump voter from Ohio who disapproves of his job performance, offered that "I know he's not taking a paycheck, you know. Thank you, I guess. But ... I thought you weren't supposed to make money off of the presidency at all, and he is so much richer now than when he started."</p><p>Shauna, another disapproving Trump voter from Michigan, shared a similar perspective, characterizing the salary rejection as a "ploy," and noting that he's making much more off the presidency than the law allows for. Cory reflected ruefully that "his net worth has increased a couple billion dollars, and I can confidently tell you my net worth has not increased since he has come into office."</p><p>Trump exploited preexisting voter cynicism about politicians and made it far worse. Gallup polling from earlier in September found that 89% of Americans now believe that corruption is "widespread in the government." That is higher than all other members of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, and represents a 16-point increase in two years.</p><p>The near-term result of voter disillusionment is very likely to be a drubbing for GOP candidates in five weeks. But the longer-term damage to our civic culture is impossible to calculate. People who lack trust in one another cannot govern effectively. They cannot solve problems. Would even a sincere effort at ethics reform — such as we saw after Watergate — gain traction in a country as suspicious and jaded as ours? It's unclear. But one thing is certain: The billionaire populist myth is dead, dead, dead.</p><p><i>Mona Charen is policy editor of the Bulwark and host of the “Beg to Differ” podcast.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-0a0000" name="module-0a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Son remains hostile even after dad's cancer diagnosis
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am a 79-year-old woman who, over time, has suffered the loss of several family members. Now I'm facing the worst loss imaginable. A year ago, my 24-year-old grandson "Rafe" cut himself off from his father and from me. Until then, we had been a close, loving family who did things together. Rafe and his girlfriend live rent-free in my son's house, yet they refuse to speak to either of us. I've written and spoken to him, but he says that unless my son and I "change," he wants nothing to do with us. We are clueless as to what change he wants from us, and he offers no explanation.</p><p>My son was recently diagnosed with incurable cancer. The doctors say that, with treatment, he can live for a number of years. All of this has been explained to Rafe, yet he remains silent. If there had been abuse or lack of care over the years, I could understand his attitude, but it's the opposite. His father and I have done everything in the world for him all his life, maybe too much. My son needs love and support now more than ever. What can I do to reach my grandson? Do I need to accept this and give up? — <i>HEARTBROKEN</i></p><p><b>DEAR HEARTBROKEN:</b> I understand your pain and frustration. Until Rafe decides to explain what has caused his grudge, his issues belong on the back burner. For now, focus your energy on your son. Support him as much as you can, and try not to let him dwell on his problems with his son. Consider that an adult son who continues to give his father the silent treatment may not deserve to live in his father's house at all, much less rent-free.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My son (51) has been married to his wife (47) for 13 years. From day one, it was apparent that she had a shopping addiction. Together they have money to support this constant waste, but it overruns the house. My son has often expressed that it's a problem. First, it was stocking the pantry, then a second pantry and no room in the fridge for even a cold drink. They have magazines that are never read, piles of books to read "someday" and every drawer in the kitchen overflowing with unused gadgets. You don't even want to know what it's like at Christmas. This has been a constant source of stress for my son. I suspect she has a mental problem, but how should we approach it? She thinks it's OK to live this way. — <i>NEED HELP IN BEACH TOWN</i></p><p><b>DEAR NEED HELP:</b> Your daughter-in-law appears to be a shopping addict and a hoarder. The good news: There are organizations that help with both of those problems. Find a nearby Spenders Anonymous meeting (spenders.org) and suggest that your son attend even if his wife refuses. To get rid of all the extra stuff, search for a decluttering service in their city. Your DIL will be anxious or unhappy about this at first, but your son can learn strategies that may bring her around.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Living slowly in the Driftless region’s Viroqua, Wisconsin
entries.summary: <p><i>Regenerative tourism harnesses the power of sustainable travel to transform places and communities for the better. In this series, we look at Midwestern towns and small cities that have leaned into tourism to help lift local economies and create destinations that travelers want to visit.</i></p><p>Stage coaches, and later Greyhound buses, long used the grand <a class="Link" href="https://www.hotelfortney.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Hotel Fortney</u></a> in Viroqua, Wisconsin, about 90 miles northwest of Madison, as a depot for travelers. The 1899 Queen Anne with a signature two-story circular bay window accommodated tobacco traders in southwestern Wisconsin’s Driftless Area where Norwegian settlers commonly grew the cash crop. As a social hub, the hotel served elaborate meals. A multi-course Easter menu in 1901 opened with “mullagawny” soup and closed with “Tea. Coffee. Milk.”</p><p>As the tobacco age waned, so did the Fortney. By 2017, when Brian Wrobel, a local organic rancher, toured the building, it was derelict even if it still accommodated long-term renters. “It was a one-of-a-kind building, and we wanted to bring it back,” said Wrobel, who with his family bought the building in 2020 and, after extensive remodeling, reopened with 14 rooms and a lounge in 2023 (100 N. Main St.).</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-5e0000" name="image-5e0000"></a> <picture Hotel Fortney</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>As the seat of Vernon County and home to its courthouse, Viroqua weathered the tobacco bust and the mid-century exodus from small towns that struck rural America, driven by industrialization and car culture. But on its outskirts, interest grew among back-to-the-landers and small farmers, including Amish families, drawn to the fertile soils of the Driftless, a rare Midwestern region that had eluded the glaciers and their scouring retreat. Its irregular, contoured fields resisted industrial farming allowing small producers to flourish (in time many of them would band together as Organic Valley, the country’s largest farmer-owned organic coop).</p><p>Over time, Viroqua became synonymous with the so-called Driftless Slow movement, or intentional living with a strong DIY streak. Driftless newcomers contributed “original thinking about how to live their lives and raise their families and steward the land and think about health and wellness and spirituality,” said Jacob Hundt, the executive director of the <a class="Link" href="https://www.driftlessfolkschool.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Driftless Folk School</u></a> (608-284-8524) who grew up on a farm in the area. “As a inspired other community initiatives including <a class="Link" href="https://www.liveinviroqua.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Live in Viroqua</u></a>, a summer concert series that takes place over eight dates and regularly draws 1,000 fans.</p><p>Justin Miller, the hotel’s lounge manager, launched the free series in 2022 through his nonprofit Fourth Stream, raising money from local businesses to pay for 16 bands and sound engineers seasonally. “I thought Viroqua would be a great place for it,” said Miller, “and I found some likeminded folks who thought it would be a good thing too.”</p><p><b>Other things to do:</b></p><p>Outside of Viroqua, the Driftless offers a bounty of outdoor activities including hiking at <a class="Link" href="http://kvr.state.wi.us/Home" target="_blank" ><u>Kickapoo Valley Reserve</u></a> (S3661 State Road 131, La Farge) and <a class="Link" href="https://dnr.wisconsin.gov/topic/parks/wildcat" target="_blank" ><u>Wildcat Mountain State Park</u></a> (E13660 State Hwy 33, Ontario).</p><p>Among scenic drives, the <a class="Link" href="https://www.windingroadsart.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Winding Roads Arts Tour</u></a> offers a self-guided drive to 20 area artist studios each June. The <a class="Link" href="https://www.vernoncountyhistory.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Vernon County Historical Society</u></a> (410 S. Center Ave.) maps out history-driven drives in the region, including an itinerary that traces the end of the Black Hawk War.</p>

target="_blank" >Privacy Policy</a></p> </div> </form> </bsp-form> </div> </div><p>Well, thank Harry, England and St. George that it <i>is</i> a musical, because “Operation Mincemeat” is amazingly well conceived as a stage spectacle. It takes a special kind of vision to read the real-life history of a World War II spy mission and see the seed of a West End farce with heart.</p><p>Impressively faithful to the facts of true historical Operation Mincemeat, the musical centers around characters at MI-5, the British spy agency. An Allied invasion of Sicily is on the horizon, to gain a foothold to retake mainland Europe. The spies hope to fool the Nazis into thinking the attack will come through Sardinia instead so that they will move troops out of Sicily and make it easier to take.</p><div class="RatingCard Enhancement" data-module data-rating="4.0" data-align-center> <div class="RatingCard-title"> “Operation Mincemeat” </div> <div class="RatingCard-content"> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e00000" name="module-e00000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>When</b>: Through Oct. 11<br><b>Where</b>: CIBC Theatre, 18 W. Monroe St.<br><b>Info</b>: <a class="Link" href="https://www.broadwayinchicago.com/shows/operation-mincemeat-a-new-musical/" target="_blank" ><u>Tickets</u></a> from $40–$150; run time is two hours, 35 minutes, including one intermission</div> </div><p>The spies devise a plan to put bogus communiqués about an attack on Sardinia in the hands of the Germans by stashing them in the briefcase of a dead airman who washes up on the Spanish coast. To execute the plan, they need a dead body, an invented identity with full documentation and an inconspicuous delivery.</p><p>The musical leans into the unlikelihood and audacity of the trickery, mining the ridiculousness for jokes and finding the caper in the historical event. Written and composed by the British troupe SpitLip, the show calls for just five actors who play all the roles. They wear black pants and white shirts and don coats, vests, glasses, mustaches and the like to identify their many changes of character.</p><p>The panache and coordination of the cast on these shifts rivals any door-slamming farce. Props and costume elements stashed behind moving set pieces appear like in a magic act, feats of timing performed with antic energy. Doors open in unexpected places (commented on by the characters in another meta moment) and the actors put on a whole new demeanor in an eyeblink. All this sparkling precision wows a live-theater audience, strongly making the case for the story as a bloody musical.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" crammed full of rapid-fire lyrical cleverness and self-aware comedy. Many of the jokes come from the vaudeville or music-hall school, where a big, fat-pitch setup doesn’t make the payoff any less funny, as when the characters worry they’ve made a stupid mistake, and one beat later another enters saying, “You’ve made a stupid mistake.”</p><p>In the lyrics, some fabulous rhyming of Hamiltonian density would reward going to the show twice. “Look up victory in the diction’ry / there’s a picture there of me” typifies the verbose vibe, as does calling the cadaver at the center of the operation a “Trojan corpse.”</p><p>It’s also remarkable how nonchalantly the actors travel in and out of characters of different genders. Each of the actors has a character they spend the most time portraying, and the program identifies them with formulations such as “Ewen Montagu & others.” Of the five actors, only two are paired with characters of their own gender, and those roles are not played for drag comedy. The actor Katie Kleiger, for example, plays Montagu as a cocky British son of privilege, the sort of cad who skates through life knowing the rules don’t apply to him. She shows his charisma and old-boy arrogance not as dress-up, but by inhabiting the character.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Many of the musical’s jokes come from the vaudeville or music-hall school, where a big, fat-pitch setup doesn’t make the payoff any less funny.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Matthew Murphy</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>That sort of sophistication, not always aiming low, points to a surprising element of “Operation Mincemeat”: its heart. Another cross-gender performer, Luke Antony Neville depicting a matronly MI-5 employee named Hester Leggatt, delivers the song “Dear Bill” with an affecting touch. When the team decides that the invented identity of the corpse, William Martin, should have a letter from his sweetheart on him, Hester takes over the task after watching two others struggle with it. She solos, composing a letter with a-little-too-real level of detail pining for Bill’s return, with the lines “Why did we meet in the middle of a war / It’s a silly thing for anyone to do.” (One of the creators reported that they took those lines verbatim from the real-life letter.)</p><p>It’s a great moment, when you can see through to the personhood of the character onstage, not just a cog in a farcical machine but also a representation of someone who lived and loved, as best we can see them through all these years’ remove. Made all the more poignant by the song’s delivery in that unique way to that unique audience on that special night.</p><p>At least it’s not a bloody film.</p>

entries.title: South Shore shooting leaves man, 23, dead
entries.summary: <p>A morning shooting in the South Shore neighborhood has left a 23-year-old man dead Friday. </p><p>The attack erupted at 6:55 a.m. in the 1500 block of East 72nd Place, according to police. </p><p>The victim, a 23-year-old man who was dead on the scene, was found unresponsive outside at the 72nd Place address suffering from gunshot wounds to the chest and face, police said. </p><p>No one else was hurt and no arrests have been made. </p><p>Area 1 detectives are investigating. </p>
