entries.title: Ben Johnson and Aaron Glenn, coaches who shaped each other, meet Sunday
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach Ben Johnson is always just off the boil, a seething, simmering study in intensity that rarely ever explodes.</p><p>As dueling Lions coordinators from 2022-24, Aaron Glenn was his friend, coworker and alter ego. During training camp practices, Glenn would punctuate any defensive stop with smack talk. Johnson usually let running backs coach Duce Staley chirp back on his behalf, but make no mistake: he heard every word.</p><p>“He certainly lights a fire under you,” Johnson said “I still remember to this day being next to him in training camp, and you can hear him — <i>you can hear him</i>. And when the defense makes a play, he lets you know. And so that shaped me a little bit as a young play caller there.</p><p>“And that really hasn't changed. That's who he is. He gets excited. He gets into it.”</p><p>Two weeks ago, Johnson faced the Vikings’ Brian Flores, the hottest defensive coordinator in the NFL. Last week it was Vic Fangio, the most accomplished. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/halas-intrigue/2026/10/01/bears-jes-podcast-tyson-bagent-case-keenum-quarterback-halas-intrigue" target="_blank" >Sunday at Soldier Field</a>, he’ll go against an opposing head coach — Glenn doubles as the Jets’ defensive play-caller — who knows more about him than either of those two.</p><p>“He's a darn good football coach schematically,” Johnson said. “And we only have three games of him calling [plays] right now. And each game, he's got a little bit different flavor. And so he's gonna make it really difficult on us.”</p><p>How Johnson calls plays against someone so familiar with him will be one of the most unique challenges of his career. When Johnson faced former boss Dan Campbell last year, it didn’t go well — the Bears went 0-2 and averaged just 18 ½ points.</p><p>With Johnson as Glenn as his deputies, Campbell reached a peak that he’s yet to replicate since their departure. In January 2025, Johnson and Glenn interviewed for head coaching jobs at the same time. Their first virtual interviews came inside an otherwise empty practice facility — the Lions had a Round 1 playoff bye — and on computers feet from each other.</p><p>The Bears spoke to both men and knew quickly Johnson would be their first choice. Glenn landed with the Jets, with whom he spent the first eight of his 15 NFL seasons as a cornerback. Campbell, who faced Glenn last week, said that “one of the greatest days of my life was him getting that job, and one of the worst days of my life was him getting that job — because you’re losing a little piece of you.”</p><p>Bears guard Jonah Jackson called Glenn one of his favorite coaches ever, calling him “an absolute leader of men.” Running back D’Andre Swift — who, like Jackson, played for the Lions — described Glenn as “phenomenal” and, in an understatement, “very vocal.”</p><p>That hasn’t translated to success. While Johnson led the Bears to the NFC North title in his first year, Glenn went 3-14, which was tied for the NFL’s worst record. This offseason, he replaced 12 of his 22 assistant coaches and took on play-calling duties himself. The Jets are 1-2 this year.</p><p>Glenn is searching for a signature win Sunday. If it happened, could you imagine the chirping?</p><p>"We were so competitive in move-the-ball situations on how we wanted to beat each other — but it made both of us better, I will say that," Glenn said. "[Johnson] is a damn good coach."</p>

entries.title: Search underway for Chicago's next Christmas tree
entries.summary: <p>Calling all Norway spruces or fir trees - the search is underway for Chicago's next Christmas tree. </p><p>Tree owners across the Chicago area can submit a tree for consideration as the centerpiece of the 2026 Christmas Tree Lighting Ceremony, taking place Friday, Nov. 20, in Millennium Park near North Michigan Avenue and East Washington Street, according to a press release from the Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events.</p><p>Tree submissions are open through Oct. 23. </p><p>Trees that are given for consideration must be 45 feet tall, located less from 50 miles from the city's Loop neighborhood and are preferred to be a Norway spruce or fir tree, according to the press release. </p><p>Tree entries should be emailed to DCASE@CityofChicago.org and should include the owner’s name, address, phone number and email address, as well as a brief description explaining why the tree should become Chicago’s official Christmas Tree. </p><p>At least two pictures of the tree, including one photograph from afar and one close-up, are also required.<br> </p>

Data center projects planned in Illinois over the next decade could generate tens of thousands of new jobs and hundreds of millions of dollars in new tax revenues, but also drive up utility bills, according to a report from the labor-backed think tank Illinois Economic Policy Institute and the University of Illinois.</p><p><b>Zooming in</b>: The state is expecting $57 billion worth of new data center projects through 2035, which the report found could create 121,000 mostly temporary skilled trade and construction jobs. Local municipalities could see nearly $300 million more in annual property tax revenues if those projects happen. Residents could have to pay $12 more per month in electric bills.</p><p><b>Proposed mitigations</b>: The study's authors have offered 10 state policy recommendations, which include the state barring utilities from raising rates by more than 5% per year and encouraging data centers to capture the heat emitted from the centers and send it to neighboring homes and businesses.</p><p><a class="Link" entries.title: Car hits pedestrian, critically injuring her in Bronzeville
entries.summary: <p>A 40-year-old motorist was given several citations after hitting a pedestrian and critically injuring her late Thursday in Bronzeville on the South Side. </p><p>A white sedan was turning south in the 4700 block of South Martin Luther King Jr. Drive around 11:10 p.m. when the driver struck the person, Chicago police said. </p><p>She was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center where she was in critical condition, police said. </p><p>The driver, a 40-year-old man, was cited for failure to exercise due care, failure to reduce speed to avoid an accident and operating an uninsured motor vehicle, police said. <br></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Bears coach Ben Johnson quiet on whether Tyson Bagent or Case Keenum will start at quarterback vs. Jets
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach Ben Johnson ruled out starting quarterback Caleb Williams for the game against the Jets on Sunday, as expected, but wouldn't name a starter between backup Tyson Bagent and third-stringer Case Keenum.</p><p>Johnson didn't think there was a wrong answer between the two. Keenum is in his 15th season, while the team believes Bagent is an ascending talent who would be good enough to start on some teams.</p><p>"I don’t know that there’s a bad choice or a wrong choice," Johnson said before practice Friday. "We’re very, very fortunate that we’ve got guys that we believe in. The whole team believes. It’s not just the coaching staff. The whole team believes in everybody in that room.</p><p>"It’s one of those things that you can’t go wrong. You just want to make sure you’re doing right by all the guys on the team and you’re putting yourself in the best chance to win the ballgame. I’m looking forward to seeing what it looks like on Sunday.”</p><p>Williams left the Week 2 game against the Vikings with a Grade 2 hamstring injury and hasn't played or practiced since. That type of injury can cost a player at least a month, though the Bears have remained hopeful he will return ahead of schedule.</p><p>Bagent would've started in his place against the Eagles, but he suffered a concussion against the Vikings and wasn't cleared until the day before the game. That opened the door for Keenum, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/28/bears-inactives-vs-eagles-k-cairo-santos-cb-tyrique-stevenson-good-to-go" >who was terrific in a 27-7 victory</a>. Keenum completed 24 of 34 passes for 247 yards with two touchdowns for a 110.8 passer rating and rushed for a touchdown.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: White Sox tab rookie lefty Hagen Smith for Game 1 vs. Guardians
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND — The White Sox will start rookie left-hander Hagen Smith against the Guardians in Game 1 of the American League Division Series on Saturday. He'll face Guardians righty Parker Messick.</p><p>Smith opened Game 1 of the wild-card series against the Astros with three scoreless innings, putting the Sox on track for a 6-3 victory. He allowed two hits and struck out one as the Sox took a 4-0 lead.</p><p>In 18 regular-season games, Smith had a 1.29 ERA, allowing four earned runs in 28 innings. He walked 16 and struck out 41. He faced the Guardians in three games, allowing two runs in 5 2/3 innings, walking six and striking out eight.</p><p>Messick went 12-9 with a 2.56 ERA in 32 starts this season. In four starts against the Sox, he was 2-1 with a 2.81 ERA. In 25 2/3 innings, he struck out 29 and walked five.</p><p>More to come ...</p>

entries.title: Chicago murals: Teens get superpower treatment at West Englewood digital arts training center
entries.summary: <p>When Carrie Pullie talked to artist Joe “Cujo” Nelson about a two-story mural for a youth maker space, she quickly knew that he was the right person for the job.</p><p>“We wanted the youth to feel welcomed, and somehow we got on superheroes,” says Pullie, executive director of Metropolitan Family Services. The mural that resulted from their conversation, she says, is “a comic book theme” that "perfectly captured what we wanted to see."</p><p>Now, the massive side wall on the building at 6410 S. Honore St. sports a Chicago skyline and suggests that the students inside are the real superheroes.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure entries.title: Man, 18, gunned down in Englewood
entries.summary: <p>A Friday morning shooting attack has left an 18-year-old man dead in Englewood. </p><p>The 18-year-old was found unresponsive suffering from multiple gunshot wounds outside in the 400 block of West 61st Street at about 7:55 a.m., according to police. </p><p>The unidentified man was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead. </p><p>No other injuries were reported and Area 1 detectives are investigating. <br></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: White Sox will rely on bullpen, 'all hands on deck' approach with pitching against Guardians in ALDS
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND – Earlier this week in Houston, entering a best-of-three series with a shaky rotation, the White Sox tabbed rookie left-hander <b>Hagen Smith</b> to kickstart a bullpen game.</p><p>To start a longer, best-of-five series, the White Sox have tabbed Smith to start Game 1 of the American League Division Series against the Guardians, once again kickstarting a likely bullpen game. With off days before each of the first three games of this series, manager <b>Will</b> <b>Venable </b>sees the built-in rest enabling him to aggressively deploy his relievers, countering the superior rotation depth of Cleveland.</p><p>“That’s one of the advantages of these off days for us and how we are built is that we’ll use Hagen Smith and <b>Grant Taylor</b> as an example,” Venable said. “We could potentially use them in each one of these first three games.”</p><p><b>Sean Burke </b>will not pitch in Game 1, setting him up to be on regular rest for Monday’s Game 2, where he could start or serve as a bulk pitcher. But even for Burke–the team’s best starter this season–getting pulled at four innings, 72 pitches and before he faced any member of the opposing lineup a third time on Wednesday, should be seen less as a judgment on him and more as the biggest chunk of work any Sox hurler can expect this series.</p><p>“Opportunity for a lot of these guys might present itself mid-game, so we just want to be as proactive as possible and communicating what roles look like,” Venable said. “Nothing different than what we’ve done before, it’s just now really all of our starting pitchers we may end up using in different ways.”</p><p>Sox starters who’ve dreamt of logging seven innings in a playoff start have to put those dreams on the backburner, but none of them can say they weren’t warned in advance.</p><p>“You have <b>Chris Sale</b> throwing the eighth inning for Atlanta [Thursday] night, like, it doesn't matter, it's all hands on deck,” said starter <b>Davis Martin</b>. “It's definitely a little unorthodox, but obviously, it's worked so far for us now in the postseason, and we're going to continue to be selfless.”</p><p><b>One big key against Guardians</b></p><p>Venable said he spent more time planning out when the Sox would intentionally walk Astros slugger<b> Yordan Alvarez</b> than he did on any other matchup of the Wild Card series, only to never do it as his pitchers held the likely AL MVP to a 1-for-8 showing.</p><p>The Sox skipper says they have premium respect for Guardians<b> </b>third baseman <b>Jose Ramirez</b>, even amid his down season, and are wary of facing outfielder <b>Jo Adell</b> with a left-hander, or first baseman <b>Nathaniel Lowe </b>with a right-hander. But there’s a simpler key he’s focused on against Cleveland.</p><p>“The No. 1 thing as you are gameplanning for this team, is if you give them free bases, they will beat you,” Venable said of the Guardians. “If we don't catch the ball and we make errors, they will beat us. If we walk guys, they will beat us. If we allow a bunch of stolen bases, they will beat us.”</p><p><b>Arbitration estimates</b></p><p>Six current Sox players will be arbitration-eligible next season, and <a class="Link" href="http://mlbtraderumors.com" target="_blank" ><u>MLBTradeRumors.com</u></a> released projections for what each will likely command in 2027, based on performance and service time:</p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-4bd68c80-bea1-11f1-bdad-5744abee5a60"><li><b>Miguel Vargas</b> - $5.4 million</li><li><b>Brenton Doyle</b> - $3.6 million</li><li><b>Joey Bart</b> - $2.9 million</li><li><b>Huascar Brazoban</b> - $1.6 million</li><li><b>Jordan Leasure</b> - $1 million</li><li><b>Chris Murphy</b> - $900,000</li></ul>

entries.title: Chicago Review of Books announced finalists for its 2026 CHIRBy Awards
entries.summary:
The Chicago Review of Books this week announced the finalists for its 2026 CHIRBy Awards.

The list includes nominees in four categories: fiction, nonfiction, poetry and essays/narrative journalism.

“Since the Chicago Review of Books was founded ten years ago, we’ve seen our literary community flourish to a level that indicates a renaissance,” Michael Welch, editor-in-chief of the Chicago Review of Books, said in a statement. “The CHIRBy Awards brings together authors, booksellers, readers, and community advocates to celebrate the writers who are showing the world the diversity and depth of our storytelling here in Chicago.”

Chicago Review of Books staff and booksellers in the city vote on the nominees. To be eligible for the awards, writers must either live in the Chicago area and/or have written work with a strong Chicago connection.

This year’s nominees are:

2026 fiction award:

  • “Tenderness” by Rowan Beaird (Flatiron Books)
  • “Kaplan’s Plot” by Jason Diamond (Flatiron Books)
  • “The Hitch” by Sara Levine (Roxane Gay Books)
  • “Every Exit Brings You Home” by Naeem Murr (W.W. Norton & Company)
  • “It Came From Neverland” by Cynthia Pelayo (Crooked Lane Books)
  • “Man Overboard!” by Kathleen Rooney (Gallery Books)
  • “Majestic Hills” by Dawn Turner (Scribner)

2026 nonfiction award:

  • “No Stars in Jefferson Park” by Maggie Andersen (Northwestern University Press)
  • “Body Weather: Notes on Chronic Illness in the Anthropocene” by Lorraine Boissoneault (Beacon Press)
  • “Great Lake: An Unnatural History of Lake Michigan” by Theodore J. Karamanski (University of Michigan Regional)
  • “Partially Devoured: How Night of the Living Dead Saved My Life and Changed the World” by Daniel Kraus (Counterpoint)
  • “Fire and Clay: How Bricks Reveal the Hidden History of Chicago” by Will Quam (University of Chicago Press)

2026 poetry award:

  • “E” by Noa Micaela Fields (Nightboat Books)
  • “The Bronze Arms” by Richie Hofmann (Knopf)
  • “Be Easy” by Adrian Matejka (Liveright Publishing Corporation)
  • “Bisquick: An American Seance” by C. Russell Price (Triquarterly Books)
  • “Orange” by Noel Quiñones (CavanKerry Press)

2026 essay/narrative journalism award:

  • “The Case for a Parking Revolt” by Tal Rosenberg in Chicago Magazine
  • “The last days of Legion Park, before the city swept it” by Katie Prout in Chicago Reader
  • “Inside the Chicago Courier Classic, bike messenger culture refuses to die” by Andrew Stojkovich in Chicago Reader
  • “Chicago Under Siege: How Operation Midway Blitz Changed Our City” by Francia García Hernández, Madison Savedra, and Block Club Chicago Staff in Block Club Chicago
  • “Chicago, ICE, and the Lie of the American Pastoral” by Lauren Michele Jackson in The New Yorker

The winners in all four categories are expected to be announced at a ceremony at 6:30 p.m., Thursday, Dec. 3 at the Fine Arts Building, 410 S. Michigan Ave. The event is open to the public and is free but requires a reservation. To reserve seats, go to: www.storystudiochicago.org/chirby-awards.

entries.title: Key education endorsements for CPS School Board candidates
entries.summary: <p>As part of our<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/" target="_blank" > voter guide</a>, we assembled a list of organizations involved in education-related work that have made endorsements in the 2026 Chicago School Board election. We are also listing education-focused political action committees that don’t endorse but are providing financial support to specific candidates.</p><p>We are not listing all endorsements, including from elected officials, non-education organizations or those that aren’t directly tied to Chicago Public Schools. Those are available on each candidate’s website.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.ctulocal1.org/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Chicago Teachers Union</u></b></a>: The largest union in Chicago Public Schools, including nearly 30,000 teachers, paraprofessionals, clinicians and school-related personnel, known for its strong focus on social justice issues.</p><p><b>Chicago Democrats for Education</b>: This political action committee was launched during the first school board election in 2024 to support “independent” candidates for the school board. The group was set up to be a counterbalance to the CTU and the mayor. It was formed by Hugo Jacobo, a heavyweight political consultant.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://cgcollective.org/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Common Ground Collective</u></b></a>: A new political action committee that is anti-CTU, heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks and says it aims to engage voters around “effective progressive policies.” The group says it wants to “defeat extremist efforts from both the far right and far left that seek to divide our city.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://incsaction.org/" target="_blank" ><b><u>INCS Action PAC</u></b></a><b> for Public Charter Schools</b>: This political action committee is affiliated with the Illinois Network of Charter Schools, which advocates on behalf of publicly funded, independently run charter schools. It is “focused on engaging the charter school community in the legislative and political process.” The group hasn’t made endorsements as of mid-September, but has donated to select candidates.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://wearelee.org/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Leadership for Educational Equity</u></b></a><b>, LEE PAC:</b> This group also donates under the name Leaders in Education. This organization and affiliated political action committee provides support and campaign services for reduced costs for alumni of education nonprofit groups, including Teach for America, New Leaders and School Board Partners, and other civic-minded organizations. The other civic-minded organizations include the Academy for Local Leadership Chicago, which offers training for education advocates and aspiring school board members. Alumni of a year-long ALL fellowship include Brenda Lee Anderson, Carlos Rivas Jr. and Jesus Ayala Jr. Therese Boyle also participates in ongoing training offered by ALL.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://onepeoplescampaign.org/" target="_blank" ><b><u>ONE People’s Campaign</u></b></a><b>:</b> This grassroots campaign says it puts “the interests of regular people before the profits of corporations and the super rich” and focuses on supporting and endorsing progressive causes.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://publicschoolchampions.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Our Schools Chicago</u></b></a><b>: </b>A CTU-affiliated group with a platform that mirrors the one advanced by Hilario Dominguez, the CTU-endorsed candidate for school board president. This group endorsed the same candidates as the ones CTU supported, plus one additional candidate, Yesenia Lopez in District 7b.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://seiu73.org/election-2026/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Service Employees International Union (SEIU) Illinois State Council</u></b></a><b>: </b>This union represents thousands of Chicago Public Schools support staff, including special education classroom assistants, security officers, bus aides, crossing guards and custodians. entries.title: Summer of change for Bulls' Matas Buzelis but what will that look like?
entries.summary: <p>Matas Buzelis remains reluctant to describe exactly how his game will look different this upcoming season, but the Bulls forward promised it will. And if it goes according to his expectations, it just might be something special.</p><p>“Obviously we haven’t played a game yet, but I feel like I’m going to have a little more freedom to do … I can’t speak on exactly what, but once it happens, I feel like there’s going to be more freedom for me,” Buzelis said with the team’s training camp underway. “Offensively, be way more aggressive defensively. I don’t really want to speak on how it’s going to be because you expect one thing and the next thing happens, but what I feel right now is I will have more freedom to play how I want.”</p><p>An indictment on how he was told to play in the past under the old regime of executive vice president of basketball operations Arturas Karnisovas and coach Billy Donovan?</p><p>Maybe.</p><p>But more likely that Buzelis has had offensive expectations communicated to him more clearly.</p><p>Donovan made it public several times last season that he wasn’t taking the mid-range away from his young forward but rather wanted him taking a good mid-range.</p><p>The year prior, Buzelis entered his rookie campaign with a Dirk Nowitzki-one-legged-fadeaway that he had in his bag from the G League, and after going 5-of-17 (29.4%) from mid-range that season, Donovan not only wanted that move out of his bag, but in a trash can.</p><p>Last season, he shot 19 mid-range shots, hitting on eight (42.1%).</p><p>A source did say that Karnisovas and the analytics department did stress to Buzelis to stay completely away from mid-range shots if he could help it, and it sounded like two different messages from two different places.</p><p>Either way, Buzelis, who felt like he shot too many threes at times last year, now feels like the handcuffs are off. Maybe because the message from new coach Tiago Splitter is loud and clear.</p><p>“I like good threes,” Splitter said of Buzelis. “I think if he’s forcing threes that’s not a good thing. I also don’t think that he cannot shoot mid-range. That’s not how I see it. Now sometimes mid-range is a bad shot for that specific play, but you just got to be smart.</p><p>“I think he’s overthinking it a little bit. Just play basketball.”</p><p>Splitter would know a thing or two about the mid-range and its ability to be productive. After all, he spent four seasons in San Antonio playing with a maestro of the mid-range in Kawhi Leonard.</p><p>To put the numbers in perspective just last year, while Buzelis put up 19 mid-range shots, Leonard averaged 9.3 mid-range shots per game in the 2025-26 campaign and hit 51.4%</p><p>“Sometimes mid-range is the best shot you take in a possession,” Splitter said. “In general, layups, fouls, corner threes, catch-and-shoot threes, those are the best, but sometimes, some situations you might have to take a pull-up three, pull-up two, it’s just part of the game. You’ve got to read every play and make a decision on what shot is the best.”</p><p>A process that Buzelis is still working through, especially with a new-look roster with three new starters from last season.</p><p>What that will eventually look like? That’s the wait-and-see. But Buzelis feels pretty good about what the result will be.</p><p>“I feel like I’m going to have a little bit more leeway of how I play than last year,” Buzelis added. “I feel very confident in what I can do.”</p>

entries.title: Della Maffiola, who pressed for change after her son died in Our Lady of Angels school fire, dies at 99
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p></p><p>Della Maffiola was never the same after her 10-year-old son, Joseph, died in the horrific fire at Chicago’s Our Lady of the Angels School.</p><p>The Dec. 1, 1958. blaze killed 92 children and three nuns at the Catholic school in in Humboldt Park.</p><p>A few days before the tragedy, Joseph found a Christmas present in the garage that his parents tried unsuccessfully to hide before the big day — a spiffy red-and-white Schwinn bicycle.</p><p>Mrs. Maffiola let her son ride it under one condition: Don't tell dad.</p><p>“He was happy as a lark,” she told the Sun-Times in 2008 at a 50th anniversary memorial Mass for victims of the fire. “I always was grateful he rode his bike before he died.”</p><p>Following the fire, Mrs. Maffiola, then 31, turned her staggering grief into activism.</p><p>Ten days after the fire, she spoke before television cameras at the opening session of an inquest into the fatal blaze.</p><p>"What can I say? It happened, but I don't want it to happen again," she said. "Everybody has their empty feeling within themselves, and we just don't want it to happen again in the future. That's the one thing that I hope, my son didn't lose his life for nothing."</p><p>The tragedy led to an overhaul of the nation's fire safety laws at schools.</p><p>"She was on the phone a lot and meeting with other mothers and pushing for lawmakers to get the laws changed, and it took a whole village of angry women, but they got things done," said her daughter, Linda Maffiola-Piatkiewicz, who was three when her brother died.</p><p>Mrs. Maffiola died Aug. 8 from natural causes. She was 99.</p><p>Mrs. Maffiola's caretaker, Virginia Patano, was with her at Resurrection Medical Center when she died. Patano told family that she smelled smoke in the room when she passed.</p><p>"We felt like that was a sign from God letting us know that my brother came to get my mom and escort her to heaven," Maffiola-Piatkiewicz said.</p><p>"I felt that when she died she finally got what I could never give her. She got my brother back, you see," she said.</p><p>A Mass marking the 68th anniversary of the Our Lady of the Angels Fire is scheduled for noon on Nov. 29 at the Mission of Our Lady of the Angels, 3808 W. Iowa St, said Maffiola-Piatkiewicz, who is helping to organize the Mass.</p><p>Mrs. Maffiola was born Feb. 5, 1927, in a small town outside of Venice, Italy.</p><p>She came the United States when she was three and grew up in a community of Italian immigrants near Grand and Western Avenues in Holy Rosary parish.</p><p>A friend from the neighborhood suggested Mrs. Maffiola accompany her to Savanna, Illinois, to visit her brother, who was in a prisoner of war camp that housed Italian soldiers who'd been captured during World War II. Mrs. Maffiola agreed.</p><p>The soldier, Mario Maffiola, who hadn't wanted to fight and was glad to be captured by the Americans, said on the day he met Mrs. Maffiola "You're going to be my wife" and Mrs. Maffiola responded "You're crazy," Maffiola-Piatkiewicz said.</p><p>His prediction came true.</p><p>After the war, the two wed and settled in Chicago in a two-flat near Our Lady of Angels parish.</p><p>Mario Maffiola, who died in 1998, worked at Radio Steel as a punch press operator.</p><p>Mrs. Maffiola worked as an inspector for Motorola Company.</p><p>"After the fire and my brother's death, my mother suffered a breakdown. There was no therapy at the time," said Maffiola-Piatkiewicz. "My dad kept the family together. I've got to say, he was strong as a rock."</p><p>In recent years, Mrs. Maffiola lived with her daughter on the Northwest Side and in La Grange and chafed at pandemic-era restrictions.</p><p>"She'd say 'The Great Depression didn't get me. World War II didn't get me. What's the pandemic?'" recalled her daughter with a laugh.</p><p>In addition to her son, Mrs. Maffiola is also predeceased by her daughter, Ann Marie Nabor.</p><p>She is survived by her daughter, Linda Maffiola-Piatkiewicz, as well as five grandchildren and seven great-grandchildren.</p><p>Services have been held.</p>

entries.title: Blackhawks missing stabilizing powers of Jason Dickinson, Ilya Mikheyev, Connor Murphy
entries.summary: <p>BUFFALO, N.Y. — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> have played a lot of poor hockey over the last four years.</p><p>But arguably the worst hockey they've played throughout this lengthy rebuild has come most recently, during their final 21 games last season and first two games this season.</p><p>They've won just six of those 23 contests, getting outscored 66-43 during five-on-five play. And somehow they're lucky that goal differential isn't worse.</p><p>They've actually generated 40.1 expected goals while allowing 66.9 expected goals, equating to a ghastly 37.9% expected-goals ratio (per Natural Stat Trick) — by far the worst of any NHL team during that span. </p><p>That's considerably worse than their 43.8% ratio during the first 61 games of last season, than their 42.5% ratio in 2022-23 (when they were tanking to get Connor Bedard) and their 42.3% ratio in 2023-24 (when they finished with 52 points) — not that any of those were good.</p><p>This descent into never-before-seen depths coincides with the complete youth takeover of the roster — the arrival en masse of the highly touted youngsters the Hawks underwent this rebuild to accumulate.</p><p>In one sense, that shouldn't be too surprising. Young players need time to develop and acclimate to the NHL, and the learning curve usually tends to be steeper defensively than offensively.</p><p>In another sense, it's terrifying: <i>You're telling me this is the future we've been longing for?</i></p><p>It will take more than two games (or 23) to determine whether the Hawks' youth can right the ship and establish an upward trajectory. Even after a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/02/blackhawks-mammoth-adversity-already-bowen-byram" >humiliating</a> 6-0 loss Thursday against the Mammoth, messages from the locker room reiterated resilient confidence and belief.</p><p>At least for now, however, the Hawks seem to be seriously missing — far more than expected — the stabilizing powers of defense-first veterans Jason Dickinson, Ilya Mikheyev and Connor Murphy.</p><p>The chaos that has reigned since their departures has demonstrated their stoutness more vividly than anything they did during their tenures. That's often how it goes with stabilizing presences; they're underappreciated until they're gone.</p><p>Per HockeyStats, Dickinson's defensive impacts ranked in the 97th, 95th and 99th percentiles league-wide over the last three seasons, while Murphy ranked in the 85th, 85th and 97th percentiles. </p><p>Mikheyev, during his two seasons in Chicago, ranked in the 94th and 44th percentiles defensively and in the 98th and 100th percentiles in terms of penalty-killing. Hawks teammates labeled him the NHL's best killer last season, and the analytics agreed.</p><p>Hawks coach Jeff Blashill has argued that NHL defensive analytics aren't advanced enough yet to be trustworthy, but in these cases, the percentiles match the "eye tests."</p><p>The Hawks did get good value when trading Dickinson and Murphy <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/04/02/blackhawks-oilers-contrast-connor-murphy-jason-dickinson-winning" >to the Oilers</a> in March, although they got nothing for Mikheyev after holding onto yet failing to sign him (before he joined the Lightning in free agency).</p><p>The Hawks then attempted to roughly replace Mikheyev with Cole Smith and Murphy with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/26/blackhawks-ian-cole-nhl-landon-slaggert-jeff-blashill" >Ian Cole</a>. A Dickinson doppelganger was never acquired; the idea was that a youngster like Oliver Moore or Ryan Greene could grow into his role.</p><p>Smith and Cole have solid track records: their defensive impacts ranked in the 90th and 68th percentiles last season, respectively. But there's no guarantee they'll mesh with the Hawks as well as Mikheyev and Murphy did.</p><p>And the 2026-27 Hawks have only four other players (Moore, Teuvo Teravainen, Jordan Greenway and Alex Vlasic) who graded above-average defensively last season.</p><p>Granted, Dickinson, Mikheyev and Murphy are all in their 30s — and varying degrees of injury-prone — and weren't viable long-term solutions. For the Hawks to become playoff contenders, they'll absolutely need some kids to evolve into strong defenders of their own.</p><p>It might've been helpful to keep a few proven veterans to shelter the kids for a little longer, though. The absence of that umbrella is glaringly obvious now.</p>
entries.author: Ben Pope

entries.title: Mental health response teams now have night time hours, city officials say
entries.summary: <p> Chicago will double its efforts to assist people experiencing mental health crises, expanding its citywide response program beginning next week.</p><p>Starting Monday, the Crisis Assistance Response and Engagement (CARE) program will extend its hours of operation to 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. Monday through Friday and add a second shift of evening staff.</p><p>“This program ensures that we no longer criminalize and traumatize individuals in crisis, but instead we offer them pathways to heal,” Mayor Brandon Johnson said at a news conference Friday at the Lawndale Mental Health Center on the Near West Side.</p><p>In May, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/05/13/mayor-brandon-johnson-expansion-mental-health-emergency-response-teams" target="_blank" >Johnson announced</a> the city would use $5.2 million from the final round of federal pandemic relief funding allocated to Chicago to launch an expansion of the program. Beyond that initial investment, the mayor said he was counting on revenue from his controversial social media tax to sustain and further expand the program.</p><p>CARE, run by the Chicago Department of Public Health, deploys one mental health clinician and one emergency medical technician to respond to eligible 911 calls involving mental health crises and socio-emotional distress.</p><p>The program is now fully staffed for citywide operations, with eight teams deployed across Chicago and two alternate teams to handle non-emergency CARE responses.</p><div class="Enhancement" Rossana Rodriguez Sanchez (33rd) speaks at the Lawndale Mental Health Center in Chicago Friday during a news conference announcing the expansion of the Community Assistance and Recovery Engagement (CARE) program’s hours of operation. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Octavio Jones/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“This latest expansion will alleviate the burden of calls that police and firefighters receive for mental health crises and social emotional distress, enabling them to focus on their core duties of protecting our communities while mental health professionals focus on mental health,” Johnson said.</p><p>CARE teams respond to requests for mental health services made through 911 dispatch or the program’s non-emergency email. City officials said 911 dispatchers may also initiate a CARE team response without a request if a call is deemed eligible.</p><p>Eligible situations include non-violent, non-medical crises where there is no active threat to the individual or others, according to city officials.</p><p>CARE teams will also have greater access to information through the city’s new <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/09/22/oemc-new-911-dispatch-system-chicago-city-council" target="_blank" >computer-aided dispatch system</a>.</p><p>Although CARE teams have always had access to police and fire radio communications, those channels provide limited information. Previously, teams could primarily see the address associated with a call, without access to additional details that could help them better assess the situation before responding.</p><p>The new CAD system will give CARE teams limited-view access, filtering out sensitive information while providing details needed to inform their response. Unlike the legacy system, the new platform can also be updated more easily, and officials will continue monitoring it to ensure CARE teams have access to the information they need, city officials said.</p><p>City officials said CARE responses to 911 calls increased 51% from May through August in 2026 compared with the first four months of the year.</p><p>Ald. Rossana Rodriguez Sanchez (33rd), chair of the committee on health and human relations, said mental health crises should be handled by trained professionals rather than law enforcement, adding that the CARE program’s expanded hours will allow it to reach more people across Chicago’s communities.</p><p>“I cannot stress how hard it is to rewire a system that was created for policing everything,” said Rodriguez Sanchez. “Now we have a system that can actually meet people where they're at and care for them.”</p><p><i>Contributing: Fran Spielman</i></p>

entries.title: This could be the moment the Bears and Tyson Bagent have been waiting for
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ first flicker of belief in quarterback Tyson Bagent was in his senior year at Division II Shepherd University, when personnel executive Jeff King and scout Tom Bradway came back raving that they’d found hidden gem who checked every box.</p><p>It was a small school, but Bagent had the arm, the mind and the personality to become an NFL quarterback. There was something about him.</p><p>Then he beat out veteran P.J. Walker for a spot as an undrafted rookie.</p><p>Then he played decently in a stint replacing Justin Fields.</p><p>Then he convinced new coach Ben Johnson and got a two-year, $10 million contract extension mostly from what he showed on the practice field and in meeting rooms.</p><p>Throughout, he endeared himself to the organization with his scrappy story.</p><p>Bagent was a high school football and basketball star who adored the West Virginia Mountaineers, but couldn’t get a sniff from his favorite school. His father, Travis, is a professional arm wrestler. And when he got that contract last year, he broke down crying as he thought about his dad growing up without running water and how many people back home he could help with his newfound money.</p><p>He's an easy guy to root for.</p><p>The Bears’ belief in Bagent could catch fire Sunday against the Jets if they’re willing to entrust their season to him. Starting quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2024/08/30/caleb-williams-wins-bears-over-with-rare-talent-but-even-rarer-people-skills" >Caleb Williams</a> is out with a Grade 2 hamstring strain, leaving Johnson to decide between Bagent and veteran Case Keenum.</p><p>Keenum was fantastic against the Eagles on Monday, but got that start only because Bagent had spent most of the week in the concussion protocol. Johnson refused to name a starter, but has said Bagent won the No. 2 spot “for a reason,” and the team has been dying to see what he can do with an opportunity like this.</p><p>Johnson said his staff was divided on who should start after Keenum completed 24 of 34 passes for 247 yards and two touchdown passes for a 110.8 passer rating in the 27-7 win over the Eagles. The offense worked like a machine as he got the ball out quickly to open receivers.</p><p>But Keenum, 38, is in the final phase of his career and hasn’t put together consecutive performances of that caliber since 2019. Bagent, meanwhile, is still climbing.</p><p>“I don’t know that there’s necessarily a right answer or a wrong answer,” Johnson said Friday. “Both of them are well prepared to play and win a game for us, so I’m excited about that.”</p><p>Bagent has barely played since the Bears drafted Williams, who hadn’t missed significant time before getting hurt Sept. 20 against the Vikings, and he has played just 13 games over four seasons. That includes Johnson using him on a play against the Bengals last season in which Bagent lined up at wide receiver, caught a lateral pass from Williams, then threw a screen pass back to Williams for a 20-yard gain.</p><p>In total, Bagent has completed 65.8% of passes for 971 yards and three touchdowns with six interceptions (all as a rookie) for a 73.0 passer rating. Those numbers don’t mean much considering how sporadic and short his opportunities were.</p><p>If Bagent starts Sunday, it would be by far the most advantageous situation he’s ever had. He knows the system front to back and would be stepping into an offense just a few weeks removed from scoring 59 points.</p><p>He also could hold the job a while. While Williams is ambitious about his return, the reality is a hamstring injury that severe usually keeps a player out a month or more. The possibility that this could be a multi-game assignment could push Johnson to go with Bagent over Keenum.</p><p>The Bears have had two main goals in their development of Bagent: an insurance policy and an asset.</p><p>Going back to his rookie season, general manager Ryan Poles believed Bagent was good enough to keep the Bears afloat if needed, and even then he went 2-2 as their starter. In the recent offseason, the team rebuffed trade interest to keep him as a contingency for a scenario just like this.</p><p>The Bears went into this season shooting for the Super Bowl and wanted a backup quarterback who could keep them on that track if needed.</p><p>But there’s also precedent for a backup like Bagent netting a second-round draft pick if another team buys that he’s starter material. The Bears and Bagent have intertwined interests in him playing well enough to earn a job elsewhere, as Poles could turn an undrafted player into a valuable pick and Bagent could earn a massive payday.</p><p>He’s been a favorite of the Bears and their fanbase without playing much, simply for his grit and likability. He backed Fields and Williams at every turn and couldn’t say enough about how much he enjoyed watching Keenum shine Monday. He signed that extension because he believed he could learn more as a backup for Johnson than being a starter on another team. And this could be the moment his and the Bears’ patience pays off.</p>

entries.title: 14-year-old boy shot on sidewalk in West Ridge
entries.summary: <p>A teen was shot in West Ridge Friday afternoon, Chicago police said.</p><p>A 14-year-old boy was on the sidewalk in the 6300 block of North Rockwell Street about 3 p.m. when he was shot in his neck by an unknown offender, police said.</p><p>He was taken to Lurie Children's Hospital in critical condition, police said.</p><p>Farzad Chowdhury, 21, has lived in the area for over a decade. He didn’t hear the shooting, but saw police cars “flying by” on his way home from school.</p><p>Chowdhury noticed police looking at a blue vehicle two blocks from his home.</p><p>“They told me he was involved with a shooting,” he said. “I feel so terrible for the person,” he said. [It’s like] you are so young.”</p><p>Chowdhury said he hasn't experienced much violent activity in the area. </p><p>In 2025, West Ridge was listed among the safest Chicago community areas for shooting incidents. The neighborhood ranked 58th out of the city's 77 communities for population-adjusted shooting rate, according to data from the Chicago Public Safety DataHub.</p><p>The rate in West Ridge was 13 shootings per 100,000 people, while the citywide average was 42.</p><p>Data from this year, last updated in August, shows West Ridge ranked 48th for shootings.</p><p>Area 3 detectives are investigating. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-dd0000" name="image-dd0000"></a> entries.title: Chicago drivers are paying more for oil changes as motor oil costs climb
entries.summary: <p>Chicago drivers are paying more for routine oil changes as rising motor oil costs put pressure on local auto repair shops amid supply disruptions linked to the Iran war.</p><p>At Norwood Auto Service on the Northwest Side, owner Erik Scheidt said the price of the oil the shop buys has risen about 50% since June. As a result, the price for customers has gone up as well: A five-quart synthetic oil change that cost about $65 to $75 a few months ago now costs roughly $95 to $110.</p><p>“When things go up, I mean, everything goes to the customer normally because it’s hard to absorb other costs,” Scheidt said.</p><p>The increases come as the war has disrupted supplies of base oils used to manufacture motor oil, particularly the specialized oils used in synthetic lubricants. The supply crunch has pushed up the cost of synthetic motor oil, with auto-service providers either absorbing the higher costs or passing them on to customers.</p><p>At Chicago Auto Repair in West Town, manager Alex Perez said the shop has also raised its oil-change prices by about $10 since last year.</p><p>“We try not to, but unfortunately we have to,” Perez said.</p><p>At Fred’s Wrigleyville Garage & Auto Repair, owner Fred Greenfield said the shop has raised its price for a five-quart oil change from $75 to $90 over the past four to six months. He said the shop’s cost to purchase oil has risen about 10% over the same period.</p><p>Prices are also rising at major retailers like Walmart. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wsj.com/business/retail/iran-war-is-driving-up-the-cost-of-your-next-oil-change-b254bfb1" target="_blank" >According to the Wall Street Journal</a>, the big-box store raised prices for motor oil and oil change services over the summer. </p><p>Still, the three Chicago auto body locations interviewed by the Sun-Times said they have not seen customers significantly change their behavior because of the higher prices.</p><p>Greenfield explained customers have not complained, in part because he considers the prices competitive. Scheidt similarly said customer volume has remained steady.</p><p>“When people say stuff, they're just like, ‘Yeah, everything's gotten expensive,’” Scheidt said.</p><p>But if costs continue rising, customers could see another increase. Greenfield said he expects to raise his oil-change price again if his own costs go up.</p><p>“The oil is like any other commodity,” Greenfield said. “If the price of eggs goes up, then the price of eggs costs more to the consumer.”</p>

entries.title: Tension begins to thaw as Bears CB Kyler Gordon gets back on practice field for 'stress test' of health
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> seem to be warming up to the idea of nickel cornerback Kyler Gordon contributing this season. He’s been practicing all week, setting up a return from the physically-unable-to-perform list this month.</p><p>General manager Ryan Poles said going into training camp he didn’t know whether Gordon would play at all this season, and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" >coach Ben Johnson</a>’s answers were terse every time he was asked for a Gordon update until this week.</p><p>Johnson gave his most extensive thoughts on Gordon before practice Friday, saying he was “more than happy” to talk about a player who was actually out on the field and that Gordon’s work the last few days was encouraging.</p><p>“He's a phenomenal football player, and we have just been in a struggle to get him out there,” Johnson said. “We're excited about what the future could possibly hold, but it's a matter of putting in a good day's work every single day.</p><p>“He's a very talented player. He always has been. It's just unfortunate since I got in the building a year-and-a-half ago, we haven't had him available very much.”</p><p>Gordon is eligible to return Oct. 11 at the Packers and must be activated ahead of the Oct. 22 game against the Patriots or shut down for the season.</p><p>“I call it a stress test right now, and we'll see how well he holds up here over the next few weeks,” Johnson said.</p><p>Gordon is one of the NFL’s best at his position, but missed 14 of 17 regular-season games last season because of three separate injuries. He was out all of the recent offseason with a soft-tissue injury, and Poles implied in July that there was a disconnect between the team and the player on his approach to recovery.</p><p>Before last season, the outlook on Gordon was bright as could be.</p><p>He was the first player Poles drafted, taking him in the second round at No. 39 overall in 2022, and the Bears made him one of the league’s highest-paid nickels with a three-year, $42 million contract extension in April 2025, three months after Johnson was hired.</p><p>At defensive coordinator Dennis Allen’s introductory news conference, he called Gordon “an outstanding player” and said, “I have a vision for how we can utilize him.”</p><p>Gordon has played 47 of a possible 68 games for the Bears and has 214 tackles, five interceptions, five fumble recoveries and 2 1/2 sacks.</p>

entries.title: Suspenden a guardia de Ford City Mall tras video viral que lo muestra atropellando a un muchacho
entries.summary: <p>Un guardia de seguridad que trabaja para los dueños de Ford City Mall ha sido puesto en descanso indefinido después de que funcionarios electos pidieran rendición de cuentas tras la difusión viral de un video que muestra al hombre <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/09/28/guardia-de-seguridad-es-grabado-golpeando-con-su-vehiculo-a-muchacho-en-el-ya-cerrado-ford-city-mall" target="_blank" >golpeando con su carro a un muchacho de 18 años</a>.</p><p>El guardia está suspendido indefinidamente, “a la espera del resultado de la investigación en curso sobre el incidente, que se lleva a cabo en continua colaboración con el Departamento de Policía de Chicago”, según un comunicado del propietario del centro comercial.</p><p>Según la Policía de Chicago, no se han hecho arrestos ni se han presentado cargos, aunque la investigación sigue en curso.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bb0000" name="module-bb0000"></a> <div entries.title: Raoul, city move to shut down 'sickening' smells from Southeast Side plant
entries.summary: <p>State and city officials are asking a Cook County Circuit Court judge to halt operations at Pullman Innovations, which has been the source of hundreds of nuisance <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2025/07/09/pullman-innovations-odor-pollution-violations-chicago-health-epa-peter-chico" >complaints over putrid odors</a>.</p><p>Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul and city lawyers want the judge to force Pullman to shut down while the business devises a plan to control smells. The business makes an additive in animal feed used by farmers who supply eggs to food company Dutch Farms.</p><p>Raoul and the city sued the business in August over the odors, alleging violations of state and city air pollution laws.</p><p>The motion included numerous testimonies, including a former employee who said his clothes “smelled like death” after a shift.</p><p>“The company should not be allowed to continue operations until it addresses the odors and air pollution and ensures that its operations comply with Illinois’ environmental laws,” Raoul said in a statement.</p><p>A lawyer for Pullman couldn’t be reached for comment.</p><p>Some neighbors <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/08/14/south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home-smell-pollution-pullman-innovations-odor-southeast-side-south-deering-steel-mills" >suggested to the Sun-Times</a> in August that the smell may have masked the odor of decomposing bodies at the South Chicago Chapel funeral home now under investigation.</p><p>Pullman Innovations, at 2701 E. 100th St., is roughly a mile from the funeral home. Yet, wind direction can push the smell throughout the larger South Deering area on the Far Southeast Side.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/2/10/23592110/polluters-pullman-innovations-air-quality-pollution-violations" >The feed-additive plant has long been a source of nuisance</a> complaints that stretch back decades to a predecessor company, Agri-Fine, which was previously sued by former Attorney General Lisa Madigan before it went out of business.</p><p>Pullman, incorporated as A-F Acquisition, acquired the plant and assets in 2016.</p><p>Residents were at war with Agri-Fine over odors for more than 20 years until the business declared bankruptcy protection more than a decade ago.</p>

entries.title: Bears practice report: Theo Benedet to start at left tackle vs. Jets
entries.summary: <p>What happened Friday at Halas Hall:</p><p><b>QB updates</b><br><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> starting quarterback Caleb Williams is still out with a Grade 2 hamstring strain, leaving coach Ben Johnson to choose between backup <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/01/bears-qb-tyson-bagent-right-decision-to-report-concussion-symptoms-even-if-it-cost-him-an-opportunity" >Tyson Bagent</a> and third-stringer Case Keenum against the Jets on Sunday.</p><p><b>New left tackle</b><br>Bears left tackle Braxton Jones is out with a knee injury, and they’ll start Theo Benedet against the Jets. Ozzy Trapilo, the presumptive starter once he’s fully back from a knee injury, isn’t ready yet and won’t play. If Benedet struggles, the Bears could turn to backup Jordan McFadden or move left guard Joe Thuney to tackle.</p><p><b>All good</b><br>Bears running back D’Andre Swift didn’t practice Thursday (the team listed him as out with a knee injury), but was back to full participation Friday and is playing against the Jets. Johnson portrayed his Thursday absence as more rest than a serious concern, saying, "Whenever you get in a short week with running backs, that's what happens. He's still feeling the effects of a Monday night football game."</p><p><b>Secondary shuffle</b><br>The Bears listed Cam Lewis, an option at safety or nickel cornerback, as doubtful due to a hip injury. He didn’t practice Friday.</p><p><b>No Hall</b><br>The Jets ruled out three injured starters: running back Breece Hall, wide receiver Adonai Mitchell and linebacker Kiko Mauigoa. Hall rushed for 1,065 yards and four touchdowns last season.</p>

entries.title: What's stranger? White Sox winning a playoff series or aliens?
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND — You know that show “Stranger Things,” the sci-fi thriller on Netflix about terrifying aliens descending on a small town set in the ’80s? It was such the rage that a dozen major-league teams held “Stranger Things” theme nights last season.</p><p>This season, the White Sox joined in, hosting “Delightful Derek” (actor Jake Connelly) from the show’s fifth and final season to throw a ceremonial first pitch in April.</p><p>But the alien monsters from “Stranger Things” have nothing on the strange things that have happened on the South Side this season. I would’ve believed the existence of giant, walking flowers with razor-sharp teeth before believing these Sox could win a playoff series.</p><p>These Sox were coming off three consecutive seasons with more than 100 losses. These Sox didn’t have anything resembling an ace — still don’t, really — had question marks all over the diamond and were led by a second-year manager learning on the job.</p><p>Sox players began talking about making the playoffs in spring training, but talking about something and believing it are different. Outfielder Tristan Peters, perhaps the Sox’ most unlikely success story, needed a little bit of time to grasp what was happening.</p><p>“I didn’t know everybody super well right away,” said Peters, whom the Sox acquired from the Rays in December. “I’d say it was probably when we first took first place. I was like, ‘We can make the playoffs,’ the way we were playing.”</p><p>That was June 10 after a 2-1 victory over the Braves. The Sox beat the then-major-league leaders on consecutive nights and took a half-game lead over the Guardians, their opponents in the American League Division Series that starts Saturday off the shore of Lake Erie. That made Peters a believer.</p><p>Sam Antonacci believed it — hook, line and sinker — from the start. Ah, the innocence of youth.</p><p>“We knew we had the chance,” said Antonacci, who made his major-league debut in April. “It was just up to us. A lot of question marks had to be answered, obviously. And then just going out there and competing.”</p><p>But like this?</p><p>The Sox went into Daikin Park in Houston, a tough place to play in the postseason, and outplayed the Astros in two games. A team that had been hard to beat at home and had struggled on the road won a playoff series with nary a home game.</p><p>Yes, the Astros might’ve been the worst division champion ever. They certainly were record-wise, finishing 81-81. And their fans weren’t fully engaged, as evidenced by all those empty seats.</p><p>But still, the Sox aren’t “The Little Engine That Could” anymore. They’re a Hemi.</p><p>“We expect to win,” general manager Chris Getz said during the celebration Wednesday in Houston. “We can beat Cleveland. We’ve proven that we can. But they are definitely a team that’s been here before, and we respect them.”</p><p>And teams respect the Sox, which is strange considering how little there has been to respect. Did we mention they lost more than 100 games in three consecutive seasons, including a major-league-record 121 in 2024? Remember that misery? And now …</p><p>“I love watching their young guys play,” Guardians manager Stephen Vogt said.</p><p>So the kids can play again. That’s great, but I don’t think Sox fans want a repeat of that era.</p><p>The Sox introduced the slogan “The kids can play” in 1999 for a young, promising group. After the team finished in second place — a mere 21 ½ games behind Cleveland — the Sox used the slogan again in 2000, and that team won the division, finishing five games ahead of Cleveland.</p><p>But it fell flat in the ALDS against the Mariners, losing Games 1 and 2 at home and getting swept away in Seattle. (Never forget that Carlos Guillen’s foot was on the plate when he bunted home the winning run in Game 3.) The kids, it turned out, could not play in the playoffs, and a very different team won the World Series in 2005.</p><p>The point is, success can be fleeting. The Red Sox team that won all six meetings against the White Sox this season isn’t playing anymore. The Yankees humiliated the Carmines in the wild-card round, and now they’re all griping about what went wrong. It can happen that fast.</p><p>These Sox are good, and they have just as good a chance to win this series as the Guardians do. There’s nothing to marvel at anymore. There’s nothing charming about them. They’re not just happy to be here. They’re legit.</p><p>And that’s the strangest thing of all.</p>
entries.author: Jeff Agrest

entries.title: White Sox players feel welcoming clubhouse vibe has brought the best out of each other
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND – In some respects, the close friendship that’s formed between White Sox All-Stars Miguel Vargas and Munetaka Murakami was inevitable.</p><p>“I mean, just look at his face,” Vargas said. “He’s a funny guy, just looking at him. I think he’s the best guy ever.”</p><p>Vargas added that most of the Spanish-language slang that Murakami flaunted during his first media scrum in spring training, he knew upon arrival. The Sox international scouting team got nothing but raves on Murakami’s makeup as they dug in on him, and asked how long it took for him to get a feel of his new first baseman’s personality, manager Will Venable shrugged and said “Like, two days.”</p><p>“You saw really early on, day two, him having a conversation with Chase Meidroth out on the field,” Venable said. “He knew more English and spoke more English than I had anticipated, but obviously still very limited.”</p><p>Simultaneously, English isn’t the first language of Vargas nor Murakami. But where such a difference seemed like it should have been a hurdle, it wound up being their point of connection.</p><p>“As an individual who has English as a second language, I think he understands what I'm going through at the moment, so it's really easy I think for him to understand what I'm going through and for me as what he went through,” Murakami said of Vargas via interpreter. “That's where I can get really close with him in the mindset and how we approach language.”</p><p>Estimating it took him four-to-five years to become fluent in English after signing with the Dodgers as a 17-year-old, Vargas thinks Murakami is ahead of the curve. But more than that, the Sox third baseman thinks bridging those divides is foundational to this team’s lauded dynamic.</p><p>“That’s what this clubhouse is about,” Vargas told the Sun-Times. “We don’t judge nobody or try to make fun of somebody for their language. We all want to be part of the group and make everybody comfortable.”</p><p>“The universal language around here is just joking around, having fun,” said All-Star outfielder Trisan Peters. “That goes past those language barriers. It's the same thing with [Luisangel] Acuna, too. He doesn't speak a ton of English. We have a lot of fun with him, too.”</p><p>Positive clubhouse vibes often show up downstream of winning baseball games, and Murakami’s acceptance process had the advantage of his signing being the most-cited event by Sox players for when they believed this team could fly past their meager preseason expectations.</p><p>But now that the White Sox season has become defined by players like Peters, Meidroth and Vargas–all shed as non-essential by their previous organizations–playing beyond their perceived potential on the South Side, where the last contending roster was undone by the opposite phenomenon in 2022, there’s room to talk about vibes having tangible impact.</p><p>“When you have guys trying to prove themselves to their own dugout or to their own teammates, it's usually a toxic culture that usually isn't going to get you anywhere,” said Davis Martin, who has been around long enough to speak to different White Sox environments. “We built something special here where you know that good, bad, or indifferent of how you perform on the field, you know the guys love you for who you are.”</p><p>The ability to pick each other up is also on display on the field. The White Sox are not thought of as the deepest roster ever assembled, but proclaimed besties Vargas and Murakami combining to go 1-for-17 with three walks in the Wild Card series clearly wasn’t enough to sink them against the Astros. Someone will need to come huge for the Sox to knock off a Guardians team that outplayed them down the stretch, but it could be anyone.</p><p>“We’ve got guys who can take care of the team for a week, other guys can take care of the team for the next week,” Vargas said. “It’s how we’ve been doing it. Any guy at any moment can be that guy. We’re all ready to be that guy.”</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: After 2026 letdown, Cubs picking up pieces as sights turn to 2027: ‘It feels like we let something slip away’
entries.summary: <p>For months, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> were thrilled with how much went right.</p><p>Even with big hurdles to clear – an early-summer offensive downturn and an avalanche of pitching injuries – they finished the regular season with the highest scoring offense in baseball, far and away the best defense in the sport and the best individual player in the game in Pete Crow-Armstrong.</p><p>And yet, team president Jed Hoyer had to explain how <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/10/01/cubs-padres-playoffs-mlb-postseason-game-2-elimination-alex-bregman-pete-crow-armstrong-matthew-boyd" >everything went so wrong</a> just two days into October, a month his team didn’t even reach after a shockingly quick playoff exit.</p><p>“It feels like we let something slip away,” Hoyer said Friday. “We let home-field [advantage in the wild-card round] slip away by playing poorly in September, especially the last week. And we let a chance to go deep in the playoffs – and really get this team playing in the postseason – we let that slip away by playing poorly in San Diego.</p><p>“It feels like we let an opportunity slip away that we won’t get back. We have to work really hard to get back to that place.”</p><p>In other words, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/10/01/cubs-playoffs-loss-mlb-postseason-2027-mlb-offseason-free-agency-jed-hoyer-craig-counsell-alex-bregman-pete-crow-armstrong-ian-happ" >the Cubs blew it</a>.</p><p>The bats went quiet during the regular season’s final week and in the two playoff games in San Diego, combining to score just 16 runs over their final eight games.</p><p>It cost the Cubs a chance to host that opening-round, best-of-three series at Wrigley Field, something Hoyer pointed to as a critical lesson from the season’s sour ending.</p><p>“We had home-field [advantage] and we gave it up in the last week,” he said. “We have a real home-field advantage here. They have a real home-field advantage in San Diego. That really hurt us.”</p><p>Hoyer – who spent big on Alex Bregman in the offseason and made win-now trades to boost the starting rotation, both last winter and at the deadline – doesn’t strike as deserving a heaping helping of the blame.</p><p>But the man at the top never escapes unscathed in this results-oriented business.</p><p>“We put resources into this team because we believed in this team, simple as that,” he said. “There were long stretches where we looked like we could be a dominant team, and as a result … we pushed.</p><p>“We traded prospects away to supplement this group at the deadline, and we did that because we believed in it.</p><p>“We fell short and let that opportunity slip away. That’s the part that will gnaw at us for a long time.”</p><p>As Hoyer is forced to turn his attention to next year far earlier than hoped, what needs to happen to ensure a different outcome in 2027?</p><p>Despite the lineup’s collective outage over those final eight games, Hoyer’s focus is almost entirely on improving the pitching staff.</p><p>Yes, the Cubs could be faced with plugging holes in both corner-outfield spots, with Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki ticketed for free agency.</p><p>But the season-long takeaway for Hoyer was that his team’s pitching was not good enough, leaving the Cubs miles behind the Brewers in the NL Central and preventing them – over the course of a summer that lasted much longer than a couple postseason games – from delivering on what they could do with the bats and gloves.</p><p>“Our position-playing group was the best in baseball,” Hoyer said. “From a pitching standpoint this year, it was sort of a struggle from the get go.</p><p>“We’re leaning on our defense too heavily, and the overall quality of the pitching has to improve. … When I think about our offseason, when I think about seasons to come, that has to be the goal, to get our pitching infrastructure and pitching quality to the level of our position-player group.</p><p>“It’s safe to say that the biggest part of our focus going into the offseason is going to be on pitching. Whether that’s 100-to-0, what that ratio is going to be, has not been determined yet. But certainly, the great majority of our focus is going to be on pitching acquisition.”</p><p>The to-do list could be lengthy.</p><p>The Cubs might have to replace their entire starting rotation, and with Hoyer grading himself poorly on how he built the bullpen, perhaps another overhaul is in the cards there, too.</p><p>The specifics of a couple bad games in San Diego that ended the Cubs’ season won’t do too much to color Hoyer’s approach to putting his team in a better position heading into next season.</p><p>But things will be different. That’s reality.</p><p>For better or worse, the Cubs team that thrilled Wrigleyville this summer and looked so capable, at times, of achieving championship-level goals, is a thing of the past.</p><p>“We have a lot of good players that are free agents. We’re not going to be able to bring back all of them. That’s clear,” Hoyer said. “We can’t retain everyone. The team’s going to look and feel different next year. In a lot of ways, that’s a good thing.</p><p>“We do have a lot of good players that are going to be free agents, and we’ll be in touch.”</p>

entries.title: La familia de Renee Good demanda a funcionarios de inmigración por su muerte en Minneapolis
entries.summary: <p>MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — La familia de Renee Good demandó el jueves al gobierno de Estados Unidos y a varios funcionarios de inmigración, alegando homicidio culposo, conspiración y otras infracciones en la muerte de la mujer de 37 años de edad a manos de un agente de inmigración durante una campaña federal de deportaciones en Minneapolis.</p><p>Las dos demandas fueron presentadas por la pareja de Good, Becca Good, y por el hermano de Renee, Brent Ganger.</p><p>El Departamento de Justicia no respondió de inmediato a un correo electrónico en busca de comentarios.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bf0000" name="module-bf0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><div class="ActionBox Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="ActionBox-content"> <div class="ActionBox-title">La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</div> <div class="ActionBox-description">Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp.</div> </div> <div class="ActionBox-cta"> <a class="Button" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" >Sigue aquí</a> </div> </div></div> </div><p></p><h3>El agente le disparó a Good cuando ella giró su vehículo alejándose de él</h3><p>Good murió el 7 de enero, cuando estallaban protestas contra las redadas migratorias en toda la ciudad. Según Becca Good, su pareja detuvo el vehículo en una calle para apoyar a unos vecinos durante un operativo de inmigración.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/minneapolis-ice-immigration-renee-good-shooting-3f2a9e26ddac9455b931fecee5989d18" target="_blank" >Un video de un testigo</a> muestra a Good en el asiento del conductor de una SUV roja bloqueando parte de la vía y tocando repetidamente la bocina.</p><p>Dos agentes de inmigración se bajan de una camioneta, con el rostro cubierto, y uno le ordena a Good que se baje de la SUV. Ella da reversa brevemente y luego gira el volante mientras el agente vuelve a ordenar, “Bájate del carro”.</p><p>Uno de los agentes, de pie frente al vehículo, saca su arma y dispara hacia el parabrisas. Cuando el carro gira alejándose de él, retrocede bruscamente. El agente, que ya está muy cerca de la ventana abierta del lado del conductor, dispara dos veces más y mata a Good, según <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/immigration-minnesota-ice-shooting-protest-cad39aa94829e1e11468e3e345af2826" target="_blank" >un análisis de los videos</a> por The Associated Press y otros.</p><p>Funcionarios federales dijeron en ese momento que el agente <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/minnesota-immigration-enforcement-crackdown-woman-shot-5158ce0838305b491c95db97b970cd03" target="_blank" >actuó en defensa propia</a> y que Good había cometido <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/vance-minnesota-immigration-enforcement-06b23b428edcc8498362be4ac656f201" target="_blank" >“un acto de terrorismo doméstico”.</a></p><h3>Una demanda alega homicidio culposo</h3><p>La demanda contra Estados Unidos solicita daños y perjuicios por la muerte culposa de Good y por “el inmenso sufrimiento que Renee soportó en los momentos finales de su vida y por las pérdidas profundas y permanentes que su muerte ha causado a su familia”, según un comunicado de los abogados de Ganger y Becca Good.</p><p>La demanda, que solicita un juicio sin jurado, también alega “infligimiento intencional de angustia emocional e infligimiento negligente de angustia emocional” contra Becca Good.</p><p>Becca y Good, madre de tres hijos, no estaban casadas legalmente, según un abogado de la familia, pero se llamaban esposas. Se habían mudado recientemente a Minneapolis de Kansas City, Misuri.</p><h3>Otra demanda alega conspiración para ocultar pruebas</h3><p>La otra demanda alega una conspiración para interferir con los derechos civiles y solicita un juicio con jurado. Afirma que el gobierno federal intentó ocultar pruebas de lo ocurrido el 7 de enero.</p><p>La demanda señala que los disparos realizados por Jonathan Ross, el agente de inmigración que mató a Good, “fueron el producto previsible e intencional del operativo”.</p><p>Describe “un esfuerzo cuidadosamente planeado y coordinado entre altos funcionarios federales y actores privados para convertir a dos comunidades étnicas —residentes de Minnesota de ascendencia somalí y latina— en objetos de agresión y secuestro, y para silenciar mediante la intimidación, el arresto y la violencia a los vecinos y aliados de esas comunidades objetivo que observaron, documentaron y advirtieron sobre esa campaña”.</p><p>La demanda nombra como demandado a Ross, además de: el subjefe de gabinete de la Casa Blanca, Stephen Miller; la exsecretaria de Seguridad Nacional (DHS), Kristi Noem; Corey Lewandowski, gerente de campaña del presidente Donald Trump, quien también se desempeñó como uno de los asesores de Noem; el zar fronterizo de la Casa Blanca, Tom Homan; el exdirector interino de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE), Todd Lyons; el excomandante de la Patrulla Fronteriza (CBP), Gregory Bovino; y 10 agentes federales no identificados.</p><h3>La pareja de Good reconoce otras vidas perdidas en la campaña de deportaciones</h3><p>La muerte de Good y la de otro ciudadano estadounidense, Alex Pretti, en Minneapolis apenas unas semanas después, provocaron indignación en todo el país y llamados a frenar la aplicación de las leyes migratorias. Al menos 10 personas han muerto en encuentros con agentes de inmigración durante el segundo mandato de Trump.</p><p>En sus cuentas en redes sociales, Good se describía como “poeta y escritora, esposa y mamá”. En Pinterest, una foto de perfil la muestra sonriendo y sosteniendo a un niño pequeño, junto con publicaciones sobre tatuajes, peinados y decoración del hogar.</p><p>En una entrevista poco después de su muerte, la madre de Good, Donna Ganger, dijo a The Associated Press, “Tenía esa forma de hacerte sentir especial y amada que yo ni siquiera entendí hasta que la perdimos”.</p><p>La pareja de Good destacó la pérdida más amplia para comunidades en todo el país.</p><p>“Mientras hemos tratado de sobrellevar nuestra propia pérdida enorme, también me devastan cuántas otras vidas han sido destruidas en estos tiempos más oscuros”, dijo Becca Good en un comunicado el jueves. “Tantas otras familias están afrontando la pérdida de sus seres queridos. A todos los que han tenido que presenciarlo, el dolor de este momento va mucho más allá de nuestra familia. Lo que nos pasó nunca debería pasarle a ninguna familia”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>
